news.title: US Federal Reserve faces growing pressure to hike rates as price risks rebound
news.text:
US Federal Reserve officials will head into their policy meeting this week confronting a resurgence in price pressures that could make their decision on whether to hold or hike interest rates a close call – and a contentious one.

Renewed tensions in the Middle East have sent oil prices soaring again, overshadowing a tamer-than-expected reading on June consumer prices that seemed to offer officials breathing room to keep rates stable.

Add to that a demand boom fuelled by artificial intelligence and the Trump administration’s announcements of new tariffs, and Fed watchers see the possibility of dissents at the July 28-29 meeting if officials again leave policy unchanged.

Investors in recent days have also boosted their bets the central bank could hike at this week’s meeting, putting the odds close to 40 per cent at one point last week.

“Things are definitely heating up in the conflict in the Middle East and, for oil, the risk of moving significantly higher from here has increased,” said Alex Payne, a senior portfolio manager at Vanguard. “The market is adjusting to the risk of inflation being a little bit stickier due to some of these geopolitical issues.”

Potential pushback

A growing number of policymakers have outlined a rationale for why they support higher rates now, or could soon.

Dallas Fed President Lorie Logan earlier in July called for modestly higher rates, citing her view inflation is not heading sustainably back to the Fed’s 2 per cent goal. Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack also chimed in recently, saying “there is no conflict” in the Fed’s mandates and inflation is a bigger concern than employment currently.

Both will vote on this week’s interest-rate decision and could dissent if officials opt to hold steady. 

“It is clear listening to the Fed officials that you have a small group – like Logan, Hammack – who probably are ready to get going,” said Claudia Sahm, chief economist at New Century Advisors LLC. “And then there’s a pretty large group that wants to see more improvement – and soon.”

Even at June’s meeting, when officials left policy stable for a fourth consecutive time, a few policymakers already saw a case for raising rates. Minutes of that gathering also showed most officials had discussed scenarios in which inflation remained elevated due to AI-related demand, the Middle East conflict or the effects of tariffs. And almost all in that group indicated that such scenarios would likely warrant higher rates.

Since that meeting, the Trump administration said it would impose fresh tariffs on Canada and other trading partners, a fragile ceasefire between Iran and the US fractured and robust AI investment has shown few signs of slowing. 

Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh has reaffirmed the Fed’s commitment to reducing inflation, vowing on Capitol Hill in July to use the central bank’s tools to achieve price stability. But his reluctance to offer specifics on how he plans to use those tools has kept markets guessing about where rates are headed – even in the near term.

At the close of last week, investors were pricing in about a 35 per cent chance for a rate increase at this meeting, according to federal funds futures contracts.

Those odds had dropped to roughly 10 per cent after Labor Department data released on July 14 showed the US Consumer Pice Index fell in June for the first time in six years as gasoline prices declined. But the drop reversed amid the re-escalation of the war with Iran.

“Roughly one third of the banks we work with are positioning for further rate increases, while the rest are hedging against cuts,” said Pradeep Bhatia, chief executive officer of Derivative Path, which helps financial institutions hedge rates and currency risks. “That kind of bifurcation tells you the market has stopped trying to predict the Fed and started preparing for both outcomes.”

Now versus later

Officials may be comfortable leaving rates unchanged on the heels of the cooler June inflation reading, said Veronica Clark, an economist at Citigroup.

If future data reports show limited pass-through from higher energy prices and rising unemployment, policymakers may opt to extend the hold on borrowing costs or even cut rates, she said.

Some officials have indeed suggested the Fed can be patient for now. But they have also said the central bank may need to hike in upcoming meetings if price pressures don’t abate. 

“In a scenario where actual inflation does not start to cool down soon, I believe that it could be appropriate to reconsider our current policy stance,” Fed Vice Chair Philip Jefferson said two days after the CPI report.

Lifting rates in July could help Warsh build credibility in his fight against inflation and may be viewed as less political than a rate move closer to the midterm elections in November, said Joseph Lavorgna, chief economist of the Americas for SMBC Nikko Securities America and a former Treasury Department official during US President Donald Trump’s second term. 

Trump criticised former Fed Chair Jerome Powell after officials lowered rates by a half percentage point in September 2024, weeks ahead of the presidential election, calling it a “political move” designed to help his election rival, former vice-president Kamala Harris.

“Going in September or, God forbid, October – a first hike, right before the mid-terms – how’s that going to look? He might as well go now,” said Lavorgna.

Lavorgna added Warsh might be able to soothe the President by framing a hike as a move that could help hold down longer-run market rates, which Trump cares about, by containing inflation expectations.

Whatever the outcome, Warsh’s post-decision press conference will be closely watched for clues on how he and his colleagues see the economy evolving. 

“I think that’s the key thing that we need to learn over these next several meetings – about where the center of the committee is on whether or not rate hikes are needed,” said Matthew Luzzetti, chief US economist at Deutsche Bank Securities. BLOOMBERG

news.title: DNC chairman accused of throwing PHONE at young staffer during fit of rage as turmoil seeps through Democrat ranks ahead of midterms
news.text:
Democratic National Committee chairman Ken Martin has been facing an uphill battle since being elected to head the party's operations after Kamala Harris' defeat, according to reports.

The DNC has most recently reported having $2 million in debt, compared to the Republican National Committee's $128 million on hand.

Now, the New York Times has revealed that the financial pressures have allegedly been wearing on Martin.

In an outburst that reportedly took place in early July, Martin reportedly threw a phone onto the desk of a junior aide while reprimanding the staffer, according to multiple people who spoke with the New York Times.

The incident prompted a formal complaint to the DNC's human resources department. Six people with knowledge of the episode, who spoke anonymously because they were not authorized to discuss internal party business, described the aftermath.

While none witnessed the exchange firsthand, accounts differed over the force of the throw. Those familiar with the incident said the phone was thrown onto the aide's desk, not directly at the employee. The Daily Mail reached out to the DNC for comment.

Martin, in a defense of DNC fundraising totals this week, said, 'the current DNC has raised the most money of any DNC without the White House in the 198-year history of the Democratic Party.' 

The party's finances are also in such shambles that the group had to put up the Capitol Hill-area headquarters building as collateral for a $15 million line of credit to cover expenses. 

A party spokesperson told NOTUS that 'this is not new,' adding 'The loan documents were publicly released in November, and the DNC's building was also used as collateral in our prior lines of credit in 2019, 2018, 2014, and many other years.' 

Despite financial issues, Democrats are beating out Republicans on the generic ballot in the latest Daily Mail/JL Partners poll.

Voters said they'd vote for a Democratic candidate in the upcoming November midterm elections - by over nine points. That's a full point increase from the Daily Mail's June poll. 

According to an exclusive new Daily Mail/JL Partners poll, the cost of living is the most cited driver of Trump's disapproval rating, which stands at 52 percent - up two percent from last month.

Half of voters say Trump is doing a 'bad job' on the economy in general.

Per the Bureau of Labor Statistics' Consumer Price Index, energy costs are up 15.7 percent, while all items are up approximately 3.5 percent over the last 12 months.

Fuel oil has increased 42.9 percent, while the cost of gasoline, across all types, has increased 26.7 percent.

And a mere 11 percent of Americans say they are 'very comfortable financially' and can easily save. The majority say they are 'managing' or 'struggling' with covering basic expenses.

Over half of the respondents, Republicans and Democrats alike, say the economy is 'worsening' under Trump's leadership.
news.summary: Democratic National Committee chairman Ken Martin has been facing an uphill battle since being elected to head the party's operations after Kamala Harris' defeat.
news.author: Editor,Victoria Churchill

news.title: Biden warned Trump that Israel 'won't miss chance' to escalate Gaza war to Iran strikes - report
news.text: Biden administration officials predicted that Israel would expand the war in Gaza to be able to strike Iran and Lebanon, sources told The New Yorker.During the Biden presidency, as part of ongoing clashes with Iran, Israel launched strikes on significant parts of Iranian infrastructure and Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps-backed terror groups in the region, such as Hezbollah.In a detailed long-form report for the magazine, several former administration officials said that former president Joe Biden reportedly believed that any pressure that the US put on Israel during the war in Gaza would lead to bigger attacks from Iran. This would mean that the US would have to step in to defend Israel, even if it caused a larger regional war.Biden's former White House coordinator for the Middle East, Brett McGurk, argued that immovable support for Israel would help contain Iran.Even though the administration told Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on multiple occasions to refrain from provoking Iran or its terror proxies in the region, he continued to blindside the US administration by launching strikes with no real notification ahead of time.Biden officials feared Israel would expand war in GazaFor instance, sources told the New Yorker that the Israeli government did not warn the Biden administration before it carried out several strikes on Hezbollah and Iranian officials, including the September 2024 beeper attack.One former White House official added that Israel assassinating former Hezbollah leader Hassan Nasrallah nearly two days after the US called for Israel and Hezbollah to observe a temporary ceasefire was a “humiliation” for Biden.However, the former administration did not publicly criticize Israel for the moves, although many times it led to clashes where the US felt compelled to defend Israel.Most notably in April and October of 2024, when the US helped defend Israel against Iranian strikes during which very few people were injured.Netanyahu unsuccessfully pushed unwilling Biden officials to attack IranHowever, officials told the New Yorker that Netanyahu wanted to attack more of Iranian infrastructure in additional strikes, and only backed down “reluctantly.”Former Biden administration officials told the New Yorker that looking back, they regret that the protection the US provided unintentionally led Netanyahu to push boundaries with Israel's closest ally.“We could advise them very firmly, and Biden did that with Bibi repeatedly: 'Goddammit, take the win and don't drag us into a further war.' But the Israelis knew we were going to defend them,” Philip Gordon, former national-security adviser to then-vice-president Kamala Harris, told the New Yorker.Former defense secretary Lloyd Austin reportedly went so far as to compare Netanyahu to a gambler “playing with house money.”But then, US President Donald Trump was elected to office. One former senior Pentagon official said Biden's team warned the incoming Trump administration that "the Israelis were not going to let this opportunity go."Within the first half of Trump's term, the US has engaged twice in conflict with Iran.In the latest round of fighting, Secretary of State Marco Rubio said that the US struck because American intelligence believed that Israeli strikes on Iran were imminent, which would have launched a subsequent attack on US forces in the Middle East.“We knew that there was going to be an Israeli action, we knew that they would precipitate an attack against American forces, and we knew that if we didn't preemptively go after them before they launched those attacks, we would suffer higher casualties,” Rubio told reporters in March.Though Trump said he “might have forced Israel's hand” in the strikes earlier this year, the report notes that Rubio's recount of the reasons to strike Iran was familiar to Biden officials.The former administration, and potentially the current one, felt as if it could not stop Israel from attacking targets in the region, but felt the need to “shoulder the burden” no matter the outcome.Gordon told the New Yorker that Washington was in a “moral hazard” due to its staunch support of Israel, which emboldened Netanyahu to expand the war in Gaza to Iran.Some former senior Biden administration officials told the New Yorker that, at least in some aspects, the Iran war was an extension of the Israel-Hamas War.Notably, some senior administration officials, McGurk included, argued that public condemnation of Israel, like that which occurred after the World Central Kitchen incident, led to Hamas believing that regional war could be possible.Additionally, the New Yorker report noted that US intelligence agencies believed that Iran would leave actual combat for its proxies, Hamas, Hezbollah, and the Houthis.It also noted that the agencies believed that the then-supreme leader of Iran, Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, was risk-averse due to his age.However, some intelligence reports generated after the October 7 massacre suggested that a small number of Iranians believed that this was the moment to wipe Israel off the map.Now, as Israel stays on alert for a new round of potential fighting with the Islamic Regime, Biden officials told the New Yorker that they blame Trump for allowing the war in Gaza to last until last October, expand to Iran, and cause regional instability.
news.author: Corinne Baum

news.title: How Israel kept Biden backing a Gaza war his administration wanted to end - report
news.text: Biden administration officials have expressed regret that the former US president's support for Israel ultimately "enabled" Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu to broaden the war in the region, according to a long-form New Yorker investigation published last week.Several former officials told the New Yorker they now view the confrontation with Iran as a direct extension of the Gaza war.In a detailed long-form report for the magazine, several former administration officials said that former president Joe Biden reportedly believed that any pressure that the US put on Israel during the war in Gaza would lead to bigger attacks from Iran. This would mean that the US would have to step in to defend Israel, even if it caused a larger regional war.Biden's former White House coordinator for the Middle East, Brett McGurk, argued that immovable support for Israel would help contain Iran, and warned against any “daylight” between the allies. Former Kamala Harris national security adviser Philip Gordon told the New Yorker that Washington created a "moral hazard" through its unconditional backing of Israel, allowing Netanyahu to steadily expand the conflict into other parts of the region. According to the New Yorker, doubts began to emerge about Israel's strategy in Gaza almost as soon as the war started.US officials were alarmed by Israel's Gaza strategy at start of warInside the administration, officials were stunned by the scale of Israel's opening air campaign. While the IDF maintained it was operating in accordance with international law, several officials questioned whether the intensity of the strikes could be reconciled with efforts to minimize civilian casualties.The New York Times previously reported that Israel revised its rules of engagement after October 7, allowing mid-level officers to approve strikes risking up to 20 civilian deaths to eliminate a rank-and-file Hamas operative.Notably, the IDF has never previously fully outlined what its redlines are in situations like these.The Jerusalem Post learned in 2024 that the IDF has set ratios. It also views the message of the NYT report – that these ratios are essentially part of a carte-blanche strategy – as inaccurate.The Post reported that the IDF's view is that the NYT report confused various minimal parameters that may exist for setting at what level different-ranked IDF officials are mandated to sign off on certain strikes – with being the final call on approving a strike.Officials questioned whether entire neighborhoods were being destroyed without sufficient distinction between military and civilian targets."We were all shocked at how aggressive and deadly it was, and asking, 'What the f**k are they doing?'" one senior State Department official told the New Yorker.Humanitarian aid quickly became another major source of conflict between Washington and Jerusalem.After Hamas's October 7 attack, Israel sealed Gaza's crossings, with then-defense minister Yoav Gallant declaring a "complete siege." "No electricity, no food, no water, no fuel, everything will be closed," Gallant said. "We are fighting human animals, and we are acting accordingly."Biden officials' pleas to allow more aid into Gaza fell on deaf ears, report allegesAccording to the New Yorker, Secretary of State Antony Blinken urged Netanyahu and Gallant to allow aid into Gaza, arguing it was "a moral responsibility" as well as "a strategic imperative and a legal imperative."Netanyahu reportedly resisted until Blinken threatened to cancel Biden's planned visit to Israel. Even then, Israel agreed only to limited aid deliveries through Rafah and, according to the report, Netanyahu wanted the decision kept quiet to avoid political backlash from Israelis who wanted no aid to enter Gaza. Soon afterward, Netanyahu publicly declared Israel "will not allow humanitarian assistance" from "our territory into the Gaza Strip."Aid negotiations became a constant feature of US-Israel contacts, with Blinken and Sullivan often negotiating the number of aid trucks entering Gaza and which supplies Israeli inspectors would permit.Inspectors reportedly blocked items including fertilizer, tent poles, oxygen cylinders, X-ray machines and childbirth kits, while entire truckloads could be rejected if they contained a single prohibited item.The disagreements extended beyond humanitarian aid.While no senior Biden administration official questioned Israel's right to respond to Hamas's October 7 attack, officials increasingly believed the scope of the military campaign threatened broader US objectives in the region.According to the New Yorker, Biden, Blinken and national security adviser Jake Sullivan feared that an extended war would endanger US troops, complicate hostage negotiations and increase the risk of a regional conflict involving Iran and Hezbollah.Those concerns emerged within days of the war.Netanyahu reportedly ignored US requests to limit Israel-Hamas War to Gaza StripWhen Netanyahu ordered preparatory airstrikes against Hezbollah in Lebanon, Biden intervened directly, warning that the United States was not yet prepared for the consequences of a wider regional war. Netanyahu ultimately called off the operation.During Biden's visit to Israel days later, he publicly cautioned against allowing anger to dictate military decisions."While you feel that rage, don't be consumed by it," he said. "The vast majority of Palestinians are not Hamas."Behind the scenes, however, the administration urged Israel to narrow its military campaign.American officials argued that a large-scale ground invasion of Gaza would complicate efforts to free the hostages and make Hamas more difficult to defeat. Instead, they advocated intelligence-driven operations modeled on US campaigns against ISIS and al-Qaeda, and even dispatched senior military officers to share battlefield experience with the IDF.Israeli leaders remained unconvinced. According to New Yorker, former defense minister Benny Gantz outlined a vision in which Israeli troops would continue controlling security corridors across Gaza after the war so that "anyone looking into Gaza would see the backs of Israeli soldiers."Administration officials repeatedly pressed Netanyahu to explain what victory would look like and how Hamas could be defeated without a political alternative to replace it.Blinken also warned Israeli leaders that military operations alone could not eliminate Hamas's ideology.When Netanyahu expanded his stated objective from destroying Hamas to achieving "total victory," officials increasingly concluded the war had no clear endpoint.By late 2023, frustration within the administration was mounting.Austin warned that excessive civilian casualties would ultimately undermine Israel's security."You create more terrorists," he said.Later, as the fighting intensified, he sharpened the warning."If you drive them into the arms of the enemy," Austin said, "you replace a tactical victory with a strategic defeat."Reportedly, everyone on the Biden team, including Austin, believed that Israel was killing more Gazan civilians than was necessary to achieve its goal of dismantling Hamas in Gaza.One senior White House official told the New Yorker that the IDF “just operate totally differently than we [the US] operate as a ground force.”Privately, officials also questioned whether they had any real leverage over Netanyahu."We tried, but we had no chance of success, in retrospect, because Netanyahu wasn't talking to us; he was talking to his own public," senior presidential adviser Amos Hochstein told the New Yorker.The administration also came to believe it had misjudged Israel's timetable.Blinken: "I don't want to hear that phrase 'two more weeks' ever again!" For months, Netanyahu and former strategic affairs minister Ron Dermer assured Washington that major combat operations were almost complete."Just two more weeks," they repeatedly told US officials. Those assurances shaped Biden's calculations."If it is just a few more weeks, why have a huge fight with Israel?" one official recalled.Another added: "We thought that this could, would, and should be over in December."Instead, the campaign steadily expanded. After operations in northern Gaza, Blinken warned Israeli officials: "Don't do in the south what you did in the north!"Israel nevertheless launched major operations in Khan Yunis before preparing to move into Rafah.When Sullivan warned Israeli officials that Rafah would be next, they insisted otherwise."No, no, no, we are not going to go after Rafah!"Within weeks, Netanyahu announced plans for an operation there.Several former officials said they eventually concluded the repeated promises of "two more weeks" were designed to delay a confrontation with Washington until facts on the ground had changed.By early 2024, Blinken had lost patience."I don't want to hear that phrase 'two more weeks' ever again!" he told Dermer."OK," Dermer replied, "I will say 'fortnight.'"Blinken later acknowledged he never fully determined whether Israeli officials had genuinely believed their own timelines."Were they being genuine, or were they being disingenuous?" he told the New Yorker. "I think it's a combination. I would take them at their word, certainly into very early '24—less so as time went on, and that was a huge frustration.” As civilian casualties mounted, the administration turned to a question it had largely avoided during the war's opening months: whether US military aid should be used as leverage.Biden's failed effort to change Netanyahu's course in Gaza WarOfficials debated withholding some offensive weapons, particularly the 2,000-pound bombs used in densely populated areas, while others urged Biden to publicly challenge Netanyahu directly.One proposal called for Biden to deliver a televised address to the Israeli public arguing that an unlimited war would isolate Israel internationally, jeopardize hostage negotiations and undermine prospects for regional normalization.The speech was never delivered.Privately, Biden administration officials would push Netanyahu on the Israeli-Palestinian conflict.“No one's going anywhere, no matter what some people on both sides want. So how does this end?” The former secretary of state reportedly told the prime minister.But publicly, the White House adopted what one official described as a "no daylight" strategy, continuing to pressure Israel privately while avoiding an open breach with Netanyahu.That approach began to unravel as the war dragged on and Israeli operations expanded despite repeated US objections.By early 2024, the administration had begun openly debating whether continued military aid could be used to influence Israeli policy.As civilian casualties mounted and humanitarian conditions deteriorated, officials considered withholding offensive weapons, particularly the 2,000-pound bombs used in densely populated areas. Others argued Biden should publicly confront Netanyahu after months of relying almost exclusively on private diplomacy.The debate intensified after Sen. Chris Van Hollen pushed legislation requiring the administration to certify that recipients of US weapons were complying with international humanitarian law. Rather than oppose the measure, the White House incorporated much of its language into National Security Memorandum 20, which requires the State Department to assess whether countries receiving American weapons comply with the laws of war.When did Biden's approach to Israel change?At the same time, Biden's public tone toward Israel began to shift.He described Israel's military campaign as "over the top," saying innocent civilians were "starving" and "dying." Privately, he warned Netanyahu not to launch an operation in Rafah without an "executable plan" to protect the more than one million Palestinians sheltering there.The turning point came after an Israeli strike on April 1, 2024, killed seven World Central Kitchen aid workers, including a dual US-Canadian citizen.For the first time, Biden publicly warned that future US support would depend on Israel taking "specific, concrete, and measurable steps" to reduce civilian suffering. Blinken also sent former defense minister Yoav Gallant a previously undisclosed letter warning that continued military assistance would depend on Israel's compliance with US laws governing humanitarian aid and civilian protection.When the State Department completed its legal review weeks later, it exposed deep divisions within the administration.According to the New Yorker, several bureaus concluded Israel had likely used American weapons in ways inconsistent with the laws of war or had obstructed humanitarian aid. Others argued the available evidence did not justify suspending military assistance.The disagreement became public after reports emerged that the administration had paused deliveries of thousands of 2,000-pound bombs.Biden acknowledged the decision in an interview with CNN."Civilians have been killed in Gaza as a consequence of those bombs," he said. "If they go into Rafah, I'm not supplying the weapons."Despite the warning, the New Yorker reports that Biden approved the transfer of accompanying shipments of 500-pound bombs after rejecting proposals for a broader suspension of military aid.Did Biden officials believe Israel committed war crimes in GazaOfficials also struggled with a legal question that remained unresolved throughout the war.Government lawyers concluded they lacked sufficient evidence to determine whether specific Israeli strikes constituted war crimes, despite widespread concern over civilian casualties.One lawyer summarized the administration's dilemma."We don't have definitive proof, but we are very concerned that Israel is committing war crimes."The State Department ultimately concluded it was "reasonable to assess" that Israel had used US weapons in ways "inconsistent" with international humanitarian law, but said the evidence was insufficient to suspend military assistance.Some officials believed the administration had missed its best opportunity to influence Israeli policy.Former Harris advisor Gordon argued National Security Memorandum 20 "could have been, and should have been, the tool that we used to get the Israelis to do things differently."Instead, he said, after the report's release, "they knew that we wouldn't."Officials involved in ceasefire negotiations also concluded that Netanyahu was prolonging the war for domestic political reasons.According to the New Yorker, Biden abandoned plans to deliver a tougher public address after Israeli officials indicated they were prepared to pursue a phased ceasefire and hostage agreement. But several former officials said Netanyahu later added new conditions after Hamas signaled it was prepared to move forward."Bibi was playing games," one former White House official told the magazine.Blinken and Austin later warned Israel that continued restrictions on humanitarian aid could trigger another review of US military assistance. Israel briefly increased aid deliveries, but after Donald Trump's election victory in November 2024, the administration's remaining leverage largely disappeared.Looking back, former officials offered sharply different assessments of their own record.Some believed sustained US pressure prevented an even greater humanitarian disaster by increasing aid deliveries and encouraging civilian evacuations.Others concluded the administration's reluctance to confront Netanyahu publicly prolonged the conflict without substantially changing Israeli policy.Blinken acknowledged the human cost of the war."How can you not have regrets given the toll that this took on innocent men, women and children?" he told the New Yorker.He nevertheless defended the administration's intentions, repeating a phrase he often attributed to Biden: "Question my judgments. Don't question my motives."Sullivan said officials repeatedly weighed whether to break more decisively with Israel, but each option carried significant risks."We'd get progress and backsliding, progress and backsliding, over and over again," he said."What about the hostages? What about Israel under attack from all sides? What effect would it have on the ceasefire talks and bringing this god-awful war to an end?"By the administration's final months, officials prepared one last internal memorandum questioning the military necessity of Israel's continued operations and warning of "grave concerns" over the starvation and displacement of civilians.But by that point, it was too late. Trump was already on the way to the White House.

news.title: Democratic Party Surges in Polls Ahead of Midterms While DNC Faces Internal Chaos
news.text: Democrats are winning polls nationwide. Inside their own headquarters, things look nothing like a party on the rise. That's the picture painted by a new New York Times report, which digs into the state of the Democratic National Committee under Chair Ken Martin. And one moment from earlier this month captures the tension well. Martin, according to six sources who spoke to the New York Times, threw his phone onto a junior staffer's desk during a heated confrontation. None of the six actually saw it happen. Their accounts differ on one key detail too, how hard the phone actually landed, though the throw itself wasn't described as aimed at the staffer. Whether that staffer was sitting there or standing nearby when it happened isn't clear from the reporting. What is clear is that Martin later sat down with HR to discuss it. Whether that meeting led to any real consequences for him remains unknown. Money Troubles Run DeepA single outburst doesn't explain a party in crisis, though. The bigger issue, per the Times, is financial. The DNC is carrying serious debt, made worse this year by a costly decision to buy out Kamala Harris's 2024 donor email list for millions of dollars. Add to that a workplace culture the Times describes in stark terms. Martin comes across as a man bracing for the worst, convinced his ouster is coming regardless of what he does, watching his support inside the building shrink by the day. Bad Timing, Given Everything ElseHere's what makes this story sting a little more for Democrats. Their national committee melting down internally is happening at precisely the moment the party can least afford the distraction. Midterms are roughly three months out. Democrats want both chambers of Congress back after 2024 handed them a brutal defeat, one that cost them the White House alongside Harris and gave Trump's Republicans full control in Washington. READ MORE: Trump's Rural Approval Rating Takes 14-Point Hit in One Month - Here's Why Yet since then, something has shifted. Eighteen months into the current administration, Democrats now lead across nearly every metric pollsters track, generic ballot numbers, individual issue polling, head to head matchups, all of it. Fox News's own polling last week even had Democrats narrowly ahead on immigration, a sign that voters are souring on the administration's deportation push. Add economic frustration and inflation worries into the mix, both areas where Democrats hold a clear edge, and the party's national numbers look genuinely strong. Just not, apparently, inside the building where its own operation is run. Get Latest News Live on Times Now along with Breaking News and Top Headlines from US News and around the World.
news.summary: A new report reveals that DNC Chair Ken Martin allegedly threw his phone during a tense exchange with a staffer, one incident among several pointing to deep financial troubles and internal dysfunction at the Democratic Party's national office.
news.author: Sagar Kar

news.title: DNC Boss Ken Martin Accused of Throwing Phone at Staffer as Democrats Face Financial Meltdown
news.text:
The Democratic National Committee is facing renewed scrutiny after an explosive report claimed the party is grappling with mounting financial troubles, internal unrest, and allegations of volatile behavior from its chairman, Ken Martin, RadarOnline.com can reveal.

According to the report, the DNC is struggling with debt, delaying payments to vendors, and navigating growing concerns about its leadership just months before the 2026 midterm elections.Phone-Throwing Allegation Sparks HR ComplaintAccording to The New York Times, Martin's "fraying nerves are showing" as pressure inside the organization continues to mount.

The newspaper reported: "In a pique of frustration in early July, he threw his phone at the desk of a junior aide while upbraiding the person."

The alleged incident reportedly resulted in "a formal complaint to the DNC's human resources department."

The report also claimed Martin has developed a "growing sense of paranoia" over the possibility that party insiders are attempting to remove him from his leadership position.

The Times further reported Martin has become "paralyzed by the idea of leaks" despite details about the committee's internal operations continuing to emerge publicly.DNC Reportedly Facing Cash CrunchThe report paints a grim financial picture for the Democratic Party's national organization.

According to the Times, the DNC is roughly $2 million in debt and has asked vendors to postpone sending invoices until after the midterm elections.

The outlet also reported the committee paid $7.3 million for the remaining assets from former Vice President Kamala Harris' 2024 presidential campaign, with the money allegedly helping cover outstanding campaign debts.

In addition, the DNC reportedly spent $840,000 on operations in Puerto Rico and Guam, which the Times noted would have "any impact on control of Congress."

Meanwhile, the Republican National Committee reportedly has approximately $128.5 million available.DNC Rejects Financial ConcernsParty officials have disputed suggestions that the committee is facing a financial crisis.

Executive Director Roger Lau told the Times the delayed invoicing request was "nothing more than standard negotiations with vendors over contracts and payment processes."Ken Martin Defends DNC Spending StrategyMartin also defended the DNC's fundraising and spending strategy in a Substack post published on July 20.

The chairman said the committee has intentionally spent money to build Democratic infrastructure ahead of future election cycles rather than allowing funds to sit in its bank accounts.

"We made a conscious decision to invest money in the work required to win in 2025, 2026 and beyond," Martin wrote. "We are converting the cash we raise into electoral assets: more people, earlier organizing, better technology, and stronger state parties."

He also defended the DNC's fundraising record, claiming the current organization has "raised the most money of any DNC without the White House in the 198-year history of the Democratic Party."
news.summary: DNC Chairman Ken Martin is accused of throwing a phone at a staffer as a report details party debt and internal chaos.
news.author: Olivia Salamone

news.title: Inside the troubled and broke Democratic National Committee
news.text:
At the center is Ken Martin, the 53-year-old party chair, who has found himself increasingly isolated, gripped by the fear that he will lose his job and relying on a vanishingly small circle of people he trusts, according to interviews with more than two dozen Democrats, including current and former DNC officials and members. Most of them spoke on the condition of anonymity to discuss the party’s troubled state of affairs.

Martin’s fraying nerves are showing. In a pique of frustration in early July, he threw his phone at the desk of a junior aide while upbraiding the person. The phone-tossing incident resulted in a formal complaint to the DNC’s human resources department.

The fallout from the phone-throwing episode was described by half a dozen people familiar with the incident, who spoke on the condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to discuss internal party matters. None of them witnessed the encounter, and there was some dispute over how aggressively the phone was tossed. Martin was said to have thrown the phone at the desk, rather than at the aide.

Martin later met with DNC human resources officials about his behavior, according to three of the people.

The Democratic National Committee declined to comment on the incident. Martin declined an interview request. Roger Lau, the executive director of the DNC, said in a statement that the bill-deferral discussions were “nothing more than standard negotiations with vendors over contracts and payment processes.”

Around the office and beyond, Martin has taken to making macabre jokes to colleagues about how long he will remain in his post, even though his term does not end until 2029. He is frustrated with the tarnished public image of a party that he plainly loves and has devoted his life to -- and that remains bullish about November given Trump’s low approval ratings.

But the Democratic Party and its allies are far behind Republicans when it comes to money. Trump controls a $400 million super political action committee, and the Republican National Committee is sitting on nearly $130 million. Martin’s DNC is $2 million in debt.

The committee’s role is not just to help Democrats win back power in the midterms, but also to lead the party into the 2028 presidential race, including by overseeing a new primary calendar while organizing debates and a national convention.

Even supporters acknowledge Martin’s growing sense of paranoia. He confronted the party’s finance director this spring over what he thought was a budding coup. And before he met with the top congressional Democrats, Sen. Chuck Schumer of New York and Rep. Hakeem Jeffries of New York, in mid-July, assurances were given to an ally of Martin’s that the two party leaders did not plan to use the gathering to call for the chair’s resignation.

Martin was elected in February 2025 to a four-year term by the roughly 450 members of the DNC, and only a vote of the membership itself could push him out.

Trust in Martin -- among both donors and party officials -- was sapped by his handling of a long-promised autopsy of the 2024 election. Late last year, he said he would not release the document. But as criticism mounted, he relented in May and released an incomplete draft that featured searing annotations from the DNC that undermined the report.

In public, Martin has all but disappeared as a face of the party on television ever since a fumbling April appearance on the liberal podcast Pod Save America, when he faced questions about why he had not released the autopsy. His lone television interview in recent months was on local news in Erie, Pennsylvania.

Now, Martin is both paralyzed by the idea of leaks and surrounded by them. During a May meeting with the full staff of the DNC days after the draft autopsy’s release, he admitted that times were tough and chided the team for revealing to reporters what was happening inside party headquarters. “It pisses me off when I see leaks out of this building,” Martin said, according to four people who heard the remarks. “No more of that shit. No more.”

Martin said he saw “a lot of down faces” and “people hanging their heads.” He urged: “Keep your head up. Keep a smile on your face.”

“My success is your success,” he added at another point in the meeting. “So the weaker I am, the weaker all of you are.”

Martin has not addressed the entire party staff since.

Last week, he personally drafted an essay of more than 3,000 words defending the state of the DNC’s finances. He held the essay closely, and it was posted jointly by the party and his personal Substack, under the @kenmartin287890 handle, just after 10 p.m. Monday.

“We must measure success by power built, not simply dollars retained,” he wrote.

Cash crunch 

None of the party’s problems are more acute than money.

For more than a decade, the DNC has transferred millions of dollars every election to sister committees responsible for winning the House and Senate. But the national party is now so short on cash -- even after taking out a $15 million loan last year -- that officials have privately conveyed to congressional leadership that there will be no such transfers in 2026.

The main topic of the meeting this month with Schumer and Jeffries, along with their top aides and the chairs of the two congressional campaign arms, was forming a huge new shared fundraising account across the three national committees -- and state parties across the country.

Even as the political environment has eroded for Republicans, money remains a serious concern for Democrats. Republican Party committees are far more flush than Democratic ones -- just as a recent Supreme Court ruling made party cash more important by lifting restrictions on how parties can coordinate with campaigns.

Inside the room, Martin described a proposal in which much of the cash raised through this mega committee -- which would include state parties nationwide -- would be routed first through his committee before being distributed to the congressional party arms.

At least some involved saw the move as a bid to inflate the fundraising figures of Martin’s struggling committee -- and to take credit for cash transfers he could not otherwise afford.

Martin offered to do whatever was helpful, though the group left without an agreement. The meeting, which has not been previously reported, was described by five people, including some in the room, who spoke on the condition of anonymity to discuss a private gathering.

New financial reports released this week revealed the depth of the DNC’s financial hole. The party is $2 million in debt, while the RNC has $128.5 million in cash on hand. The party that holds the White House almost always raises more money into its party coffers, but this year’s chasm is extraordinarily large.

Ahead of the DNC’s July report, there were signs of trying to brighten the appearance of the books. The committee, for instance, transferred $1 million from an account dedicated to the 2028 national convention back to the party.

Some of the problems are a hangover from 2024. While Vice President Kamala Harris raised record sums that year, her loss left many big Democratic donors disillusioned with the party. Her campaign also had millions in debt that the DNC spent much of last year paying off, with Harris’ help.

Last fall, Martin sent $3 million each to Democrats in Virginia and New Jersey for their governor’s races, betting that victories would reinvigorate fundraising for the DNC. The $15 million loan was timed to allow those transfers.

The DNC has since paid more than $700,000 in interest on that loan, averaging more than $75,000 per month, federal records show. Party officials are now reckoning with the fact that they must begin to repay $1.66 million of the loan’s principal per month starting in January, according to the loan’s terms.

“Ken needs help -- H-E-L-P,” said Donna Brazile, a veteran DNC member who has twice served as acting party chair. “And if he’s reluctant to say it, I’m here to help him ask. It’s hard. It’s very difficult.”

Tense talks 

The same day that Martin spoke at the all-staff meeting in May, he urgently tried to get in touch with the party’s finance chair, Chris Korge.

Korge had been speaking with other senior party officers about a potential emergency meeting to discuss the party’s sagging finances. Hearing about the calls, Martin seemed to fear that a coup was afoot.

They connected late one Tuesday night.

“It started off extremely heated,” Korge recalled of their conversation. “Because he came into that call thinking my intention was motivated to take some sort of action to remove him, and that was the furthest thing from the truth.”

Word of the confrontation, which has not previously been reported, spread across the senior ranks of the party. Korge now describes it as simply “a family fight” that was resolved amicably by the end of the call. “I have believed in Ken’s priorities from Day 1 for the party,” he said.

The meeting of top party officers that Korge had wanted took place in Pittsburgh in June. There, they were presented for the first time with nondisclosure agreements, which Axios has previously reported.

The NDAs were yet another sign of Martin’s narrowing circle of trust.

 Strategy doubts 

Before Martin ascended to the national party leadership in early 2025, he had served for 14 years as the head of the Minnesota Democrats, during which time his party never lost a statewide race.

Inside the DNC, he led the state party chairs group. The alliances he forged there helped him overcome opposition from prominent Democrats in Washington, including Schumer and Jeffries, to win the national party post.

Martin knew the new job would be hard, frequently making a joke comparing his role to a fire hydrant and everyone else to a dog.

But Martin believes deeply in handing money and relinquishing power to the states. He increased their monthly allotments from the national party, especially in red states, and last year sent an extra $100,000 to Mississippi Democrats before a special election that broke a legislative Republican supermajority.

“We were able to -- with the extra help our candidates needed -- get over the finish line,” said Mikel Bolden, the executive director of the Mississippi Democratic Party, crediting Martin.

Martin and his allies frequently note that fundraising has been stronger than the last time the party was out of power in 2018. But some Democrats, both inside and outside the committee, are questioning where exactly all the money has gone.

The single biggest expense in the Martin era was $7.3 million to buy the remnants of Harris’ campaign list from her failed 2024 bid. Harris’ PAC used the money to cover additional remaining debts.

Martin’s pledge to increase monthly handouts to state parties has been the centerpiece of his spending agenda. But his inclusion of the territories has caused consternation.

Spending from the DNC and an affiliated fundraising committee for Guam, Puerto Rico, the Northern Marianas, the Virgin Islands and American Samoa has reached about $840,000 since the beginning of last year, federal records show -- far more than in the past.

None of those territories will have any impact on control of Congress.

The American entertainer has been open about her Democratic views, supporting Kamala Harris in the 2024 presidential election, Joe Biden in 2020 and Hillary Clinton in 2016. She is currently dating former Canadian Prime Minister Justin Trudeau.

Perry joins a group of artists who have condemned the Trump administration for using their music or art for social media posts in various government departments’ accounts without their consent to promote messages they do not identify with, including Olivia Rodrigo, Sabrina Carpenter and Kids Can Press, publisher of children’s book series Franklin the Turtle.

Many popular artists, including Bruce Springsteen, Neil Young, Adele and Rihanna, have also objected to President Donald Trump’s use of their music during his political rallies.

news.title: Questions for Tom Rosenstiel and the Students at the Philip Merrill School of Journalism
news.text:
In a couple of weeks, Tom Rosenstiel will release his new book, The Next Journalism: How the Press Must Change to Serve Democracy. Rosenstiel is the head of the Philip Merrill College of Journalism at the University of Maryland. His resume from the school website is quite impressive: 

Eleanor Merrill Scholar on the Future of Journalism; Professor of the PracticeTom Rosenstiel, former executive director of the American Press Institute, joined the Philip Merrill College of Journalism in Fall 2021. He was appointed to the rank of Professor of the Practice in August 2023. Rosenstiel, who left API after leading the organization since 2013, is one of the world’s most recognized thought leaders about journalism, media, technology, and the intersection of media and politics. He teaches courses on the role of journalism in a democracy, news-delivery models, media innovation, and the intersection of media and politics.

 With those kinds of credentials, I’m sure Rosenstiel won’t mind me, a fellow journalist, asking him a question. First, a couple of relevant facts. The Philip Merrill College of Journalism is named after Philip Merrill, who was the owner of Washingtonian magazine since 1979. Philip Merrill passed away in 2006 and was succeeded by his daughter Cathy Merrill, who took over Washingtonian. Cathy Merrill is the CEO and president of Washingtonian Media.

 Here’s the question I’d like to ask Tom Rosenstiel and his students: Why did Washingtonian magazine recently spike a planned profile of me? A profile that writer Cathy Alter had begged me to do for six years?

 I’ll tell you my theory. They killed it because I exposed a lot of nasty stuff about the left and their plot against Brett Kavanaugh, stuff the journalists at Washingtonian (and elsewhere) do not want coming to light. I also suspect that despite all of his books, degrees, experience and credentials, Tom Rosenstiel will not have the guts to answer that question. He won’t even reply to this post.

 Still, I’d like to ask Rosenstiel, the top dog of the Philip Merrill College of Journalism, why Cathy Merrill, panjandrum of Washingtonian Media, why her magazine, Washingtonian, killed a profile of me when it was on the brink of being published. Because whatever that is, it is not journalism. It's censorship.

 Hot Air readers know I was one of the targets of the Kavanaugh plot, and that I have written about it a lot, but this is much bigger than me. The Washingtonian story was killed because the editors and their friends did not want to address the bigger picture of what happened and the leads I gave them. They acted like Stasi censors, not as journalists. I’m addressing this post largely to Tom Rosenstiel’s students, because frankly I doubt that Rosenstiel himself has the guts to answer me. At least David Enrich at the New York Times had the stones to apologize to me.

 Over a year ago I finally agreed to talk to Cathy Alter, who had been pestering me for six years to submit to an interview for Washingtonian. I knew part of the topic would be about my involvement in the 2018 Brett Kavanaugh nomination circus, when a woman named Christine Blasey Ford claimed that Kavanaugh had sexually assaulted her in 1982 and that I had witnessed it. Still, Alter wanted more and I gave it to her. Alter and I met at Georgetown University, and she asked me non-political questions - what frightened me, what my family was like growing up, what girls I dated in high school at Georgetown Prep, where I was friends with Kavanaugh. We met two more times and I drove here around the places in Maryland where I spent my youth. More than once she said that she has known for decades that while I’m a flawed person, I’m also a kind one.

 I also gave Alter the dirt on the Blasey Ford hit. As I explain in my book The Devil’s Triangle, it was an opposition research operation from the start, with Blasey Ford working with researchers, journalists, oppo researchers and politicians like Kamala Harris. The story was broken in September 2018 by Ryan Grim, the same person who would later disgrace himself defending Graham Platner to the teeth. Grim’s story appeared in The Intercept, which is owned and funded byPierre Omydiar, a far-left billionaire and a member of the Deep State High School. Blasey Ford’s best friend who helped set the whole thing up was a woman named Monica McLean, a 20-year FBI veteran who will no longer speak to Ford. McLean cut off ties when it became clear that Ford was involved in extortion, slander, and witness tampering. McLean’s attorney was David Laufman, a Deep State ghoul who is now under investigation by Joe diGenova. 

 On March 31 of this year, I got a text from Cathy:

Hey there. I wanted to tell you as soon as I heard (in a phone call today with the editor), Washingtonian is killing the story. I’m tied up now with a list of crap to finish but I wanted to let you know. How about I take some of my kill fee and treat you to a fancy meal? I’m really sorry. And really disappointed.

 Cathy Alter made the mistake of making me look human. In the pages of the Washingtonian, the friend of Brett Kavanaugh who exposed the media in his book The Devil’s Triangle can’t be made to look human. More importantly, the things he revealed cannot be printed. Best to stick to profiles of transgender politicians and profiles of Debra Katz - the simian lawyer for Christine Blasey Ford.

 In The Next Journalism, Rosenstiel lays out a series of new rules, ethical guidelines and practices journalists need to adopt. Here is #1: “Journalists must begin to place the public at the center of their work, not treat them as passive bystanders to it. To do this, journalists must judge their work by a new standard—the value it provides the public, not the attention it generates. Their portrayal of the world must become less random and alarmist and more comprehensive and accurate. And they must begin to consider and track how each piece of content actually helps people, both in the moment and more richly over time.”

 I’ll tell Tom some content that could help me more richly over time. Have your students try and find answers to the questions I’ve brought up. Rosenstiel himself asked a smart question in 2018 when he interviewed Ruth Marcus, then of the Washington Post and working on a book about Kavanaugh. Why, Rosenstiel asked, did Senator Diane Feinstein, one of the first people Ford talked to about Kavanaugh, advise Ford not to go forward? Marcus gives a nonsense answer, when the truth is obvious. Feinstein knew the story was crap and that Ford and her handlers are involved in illegal activity. She didn't want to get burned by people claiming me and Kavanaugh were drugging and gang raping girls.

 In the fall of 2018 I received a disgusting, obsequious email from Ruth Marcus at the Washington Post. Marcus wanted to interview me for a book she was working on about the Kavanaugh nomination. “I am open-minded about what transpired and want to write as full and fair a book as possible,” she wrote. Yet Marcus was unwilling to answer a very simple question I posed. Christine Blasey Ford had years and years, and the entire summer of 2018, to contact me if she wanted to ask me about Brett Kavanaugh and high school. Why didn’t she? In her Supreme Ambition, Marcus addresses it this way: “One possibility: Ford would call Mark Judge, remind Judge of what had happened, tell him to call Kavanaugh, and advise him to spare his family the ordeal. She dug up Judge’s Twitter handle but wasn’t sure how to go about contacting him.”

 What? “She dug up Judge’s Twitter handle but wasn’t sure how to go about contacting him.” I’m a journalist who has written for most major publications and many minor ones. I’ve been on Fox several times, CNN and EWTN. I’m on Facebook, Instagram and Twitter. Ford didn’t know how to contact me? And Marcus believed this? I have since tried to call Marcus several times. She won't pick up her phone.

 When Marcus was promoting Supreme Ambition at its launch, Rosenstiel was in the audience. Yet it was not him but an audience member at a book signing who stood up and noted that since 2018 no one has ever come forward to corroborate Ford’s story - this despite the fact that Marcus claims in D.C. “everybody leaks.” “Well there was no investigation,” Marcus said. Her questioner was not impressed: “But you investigated!” She had just published a book about it!

 I have one final request for Tom Rosenstiel, King of Journalism at the Philip Merrill College of Journalism at the University of Maryland. Cathy Alter recorded our interview at Georgetown University, then printed it into a 28,000-word transcript. Does Rosenstiel or one of his students have enough journalistic curiosity to simply ask that the audio and transcript of the interview, full and unedited, be released to the public?

 That’s what I thought.

news.title: Katy Perry slams White House for using her ‘Firework’ song in Iran war video
news.text:
Katy Perry lambasted the Trump administration over the weekend for using her song “Firework” in one of its social media videos about U.S airstrikes on Iran.

The pop star said she was “deeply appalled and angry” over the use of her song in a White House TikTok video featuring bombs exploding set to Perry’s 2010 hit — specifically featuring her lyrics “boom, boom, boom.” A caption on the video, which has more than 6 million views, reads: “Iran has been warned.”

“I did not approve this, I was not asked, and I absolutely do not condone it. I wrote this song to be an anthem of hope, healing, and inner strength for people going through their darkest personal moments,” Perry wrote in an X post on Saturday. “To see a message of self-worth and upliftment weaponized to soundtrack destruction and violence is a complete violation of everything my song stands for. My music is for bringing people together, not celebrating warfare.”

White House aide Kaelan Dorr responded to Perry, saying, “This you?” He posted Perry’s own military-themed music video of her song “Part of Me,” in which she’s dressed in combat uniform.

Perry, who is in a romantic relationship with former Canadian Prime Minister Justin Trudeau, is among many other prominent artists who have rebuked the Trump administration for using their music in videos on official accounts.

Kesha publicly admonished President Donald Trump’s administration in March after the official White House TikTok account used her song “Blow” in another video about military action. “Stop using my music, perverts,” she said on X.

https://twitter.com/KeshaRose/status/2028636354150572457?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw%7Ctwcamp%5Etweetembed%7Ctwterm%5E2028636354150572457%7Ctwgr%5E4ecbd359b28f4420e045c29ccf61777045b6a7b6%7Ctwcon%5Es1_&ref_url=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.them.us%2Fstory%2Fkesha-slams-white-house-using-blow-in-video-promoting-war

The Filipino American pop star Olivia Rodrigo expressed outrage at the Trump administration after it used her song “All-American Bitch” last fall in a video threatening deportations. She responded to the Department of Homeland Security at the time, saying, “Don’t ever use my songs to promote your racist, hateful propaganda.” 

While the video is still visible, Rodrigo’s music has been removed.

And last December, Sabrina Carpenter condemned the administration for using her song “Juno” in a video about immigration arrests, which she called “evil and disgusting.”“Do not ever involve me or my music to benefit your inhumane agenda,” the singer wrote at the time.

Ariana Grande also posted on her Instagram story last September criticizing the administration over its immigration policy, anti-LGBTQ+ messaging and alleged censorship. In response, White House Deputy Press Secretary Kush Desai told her, “Save your tears,” a reference to one of her songs. Last month, after the White House used her song “Bye” in an anti-immigration video on TikTok, she commented, “Please do not ever use my music ⁠in relation to this barbaric, inhumane, heinous nonsense.”

Trump has repeatedly lashed out at Taylor Swift. The White House poked fun at the mega star earlier this month when shemarried Kansas City Chiefs player Travis Kelce at Madison Square Garden. Its official X account posted photo-shopped images of the venue’s billboards blaring, “TRUMP IS YOUR PRESIDENT.” After she endorsed his opponent, Kamala Harris, in the 2024 election, Trump wrote, “I HATE TAYLOR SWIFT!”

Last year, Trump went after Bruce Springsteen for insulting the president at a concert in Manchester, England, where the Boss called the administration “corrupt, incompetent and treasonous.” Trump called the Grammy-award winning artist “highly overrated,” writing in part, “Never liked him, never liked his music, or his Radical Left Politics and, importantly, he’s not a talented guy.”

news.title: Minn. Lawmaker Says Angie Craig Sought His Endorsement As He Was In ICU After Assassination Attempt
news.text:
WASHINGTON — Minnesota Democratic state Sen. John Hoffman said Rep. Angie Craig (D-Minn.) was trying to get his endorsement in her Senate bid as he was recovering from being shot nine times in an attempted assassination in June 2025.

Craig is calling his claim “categorically false.”

Hoffman and his wife, Yvette, were shot multiple times by Vance Luther Boelter, who was just sentenced on Thursday to two consecutive life terms plus a consecutive 40-year term for attempting to murder the Hoffmans, and for murdering the late Minnesota Democratic state Rep. Melissa Hortman and her husband, Mark.

Speaking Friday night at a St. Paul campaign event for Craig’s primary opponent, Democratic Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan, Hoffman said a stark difference between the two is how they reached out to him after he’d been shot.

“When her opponent would check on our family, she asked for my — she asked that I endorse her campaign,” Hoffman said to boos in the crowd. “She sent a dear friend out twice, once when I was in the ICU and once at our home. Honest to God, true story. And I’m being public about it because it really hurt.”

He claimed Craig was eager for his endorsement at the time because it was at a moment “when our family’s story had high visibility.”

“That’s all you need to know about the differences between the opponent that Peggy has and Peggy Flanagan,” said Hoffman, raising his voice, “because Peggy Flanagan, she checked on us out of her love for how we were.”

Late Friday, Yvette Hoffman shared a social media post by a Minnesota influencer relaying the story of Craig seeking her husband’s endorsement when he was in the ICU.

“It’s true,” she wrote.

A Craig campaign spokesperson disputed Hoffman’s story.

“We cannot imagine the pain and trauma that the entire Hoffman family has and continue to experience. But the claim is categorically false,” Craig’s spokesperson said in a statement.

“The Congresswoman reached out to Senator Hoffman only expressing deep sympathy from her and her wife, Cheryl, after their horrific shooting while he was in the ICU and did not reach out again until August 5 after he began making political endorsements in other races again,” said the spokesperson, sharing a link to this story about Hoffman endorsing a congressional candidate in August 2025. “The Congresswoman continues to pray and keeps John, Yvette and Hope Hoffman in her thoughts and is grateful for their continued recovery.”

Her campaign also shared a screenshot of text messages the congresswoman sent to Hoffman after his attempted assassination.

In one, sent on the day of the assassination attempt, Craig says she and her wife are praying for him and his wife. In another, sent weeks later, she says she would “love to talk with you about the open Senate race when you’re up to it.”

Hoffman declined to be interviewed for this story.

But Minnesota Democratic state Sen. Erin Maye Quade told HuffPost she had his permission to speak on his behalf and said when she visited him in a rehab facility he was in after he’d left the ICU, Hoffman told her about Craig sending a surrogate to the ICU to get his endorsement.

“He told me about it in real time,” said Maye Quade. “He was telling me about baskets people had sent, or people who had come to see him at the hospital, and he mentioned, ‘Yeah, so and so came and saw me and was talking about endorsing Angie Craig.’”

She said she told Hoffman at the time that that was “so inappropriate” and that he agreed it was “super weird.” He also said the Craig campaign surrogate “felt really weird about it.”

As for Craig denying this happened, Maye Quade said, “It’s one thing to have disagreements on who we’re endorsing and stuff. But to call John Hoffman a liar is, I think, it’s worse than the original faux pas.”

Craig and Flanagan are in a heated race to replace Sen. Tina Smith (D-Minn.), who is not running for reelection. Flanagan, a staunch progressive who overwhelmingly earned her state party’s endorsement in May, has made it central to her campaign that she doesn’t take money from corporate PACs, and has attacked Craig for benefiting from cryptocurrency and pro-Israel groups spending millions of dollars on ads in support of her campaign.

She’s also railed against Craig’s voting record on immigration, an explosive issue in Minnesota after the Trump administration’s surge of Immigration and Customs Enforcement officers here late last year traumatized immigrant communities and left Alex Pretti and Renee Good dead.

Craig, a moderate four-term congresswoman who flipped her district from red to blue in 2018, has touted legislation she’s passed in the House and her record of being able to work with Republicans. She’s also argued she has the “electability” factor and that Flanagan is vulnerable in a general election because of the governor’s ties to Minnesota’s fraud scandal.

Both are vying to win the Democratic primary election on Aug. 11. Minnesota, a state that Democratic presidential nominee Kamala Harris carried by 4.2 percentage points in 2024, hasn’t sent a Republican to the U.S. Senate in 20 years, which means whoever wins the Democratic primary is strongly favored to win the November general election.

news.title: DNC chair threw phone in frustration as strains for Democrats show ahead of midterms, report says
news.text:
The Democratic Party’s national office is reportedly wracked by internal politics, an unsteady leader and deep financial problems even as Democratic politicians nationwide appear to be on an upswing.

A new report from The New York Times out Sunday detailed the sheer scale of the party’s debts and financial burdens, which this past year included a major multimillion-dollar buyout of Kamala Harris’s 2024 campaign donor email list. It also painted an image of a brutal work atmosphere where the boss, Democratic National Committee Chair Ken Martin, is reportedly petrified of losing his job, certain his doom is prewritten, and surrounded by a shrinking number of loyalists.

In particular, the Times report revealed an incident that is alleged to have occurred earlier this month, during a heated discussion between Martin and a junior staffer. During the conversation, Martin is reported to have “thrown” his phone onto the staffer’s desk, in a manner described as not aimed at the staffer themself. It wasn’t immediately clear, from the Times’s reporting, whether the staffer was seated at the desk or standing nearby when the “upbraiding” occurred, but the incident was described to the newspaper by six sources. Martin later met with human resources personnel over the incident, according to the Times, but it was not clear if he was formally disciplined in any way.

The paper further described the accounts of the incident as varying in their judgement of how hard Martin threw the phone, and none of the sources reportedly witnessed the incident firsthand.

DNC press officials declined to comment to the Times regarding the incident, and did not immediately respond to a request for comment from The Independent.

Martin’s reported troubles come at an inopportune time for Democrats nationally, who are on the rebound and would likely prefer it if the DNC were not focused on navigating internal issues. The midterm elections are just over three months away, and the party is making a play at retaking majorities in both houses of Congress after suffering a crushing defeat in 2024 alongside Harris’s defeat, handing unified control of government over to Republicans aligned with Trump’s second administration.

After a year and a half of that administration in power, Democrats have retaken advantages across all available polling, including on generic ballot surveys, issue-based polling and general election matchup gauging. A Fox poll released this past week showed the party winning voters by a slim margin on the issue of immigration, signalling Americans’ deep discontent with the White House’s deportation strategies, while Democrats held clear advantages on a host of other issues including the most important two: the economy and inflation.

Meanwhile, a Washington Post report out Sunday reveals a major enthusiasm problem sapping Republican strength ahead of the midterms, where one in five “reliable” GOP voters are now considering staying home or even voting Democrat, according to the Koch-linked AFP Action PAC. The group’s surveys revealed high levels of dissatisfaction over the administration’s war with Iran and its effect on gas prices and other sectors of the economy, and a sense of betrayal sinking in across Republican voters which the White House has very publicly denied.

Republicans can afford to lose three seats in the Senate this fall and still cling to a majority within the chamber. But Democrats are rallying and hold advantages in several states where Republican senators currently hold seats, including North Carolina and Ohio. Several others – Maine, Texas and Alaska – are extremely close.

Part of the reason for Republicans’ woes has been the interference of Donald Trump. The president endorsed against two sitting GOP senators this cycle, engineering the defeats of both, and his approval ratings remain hovering near their lowest recorded point across his entire political career.

The Post reported that Trump was confronted by a senior Republican senator about his unpopularity and GOP voter enthusiasm issues at a recent meeting in the Oval Office.

Trump reportedly responded by telling the senator that passing the SAVE America Act, a piece of voter ID legislation which is currently the president’s top priority, would solve that issue.

Most analysts are unconvinced, and note that polling has shown that more than four in 10 voters are unsure of whether or not they support that bill, a larger share than its supporters or opponents.
news.summary: Ken Martin threw phone on staffer’s desk, according to The New York Times
news.author: John Bowden

Loomer had spent years minimizing the war and amplifying Russian propaganda until she made a dramatic reversal this week.

“I’ve come to realize I was bamboozled by Russian propaganda and I came to believe a lot of untrue things about Ukraine. I used to think that this was a country full of Nazis,” Loomer told Zelenskyy as she interviewed him for her show on Rumble, an online video platform.

Loomer blamed her indoctrination on getting banned by American social media platforms, leading her to try Telegram, where Russian media is widely shared.

“The Russians,” she added, “are very good at capitalizing on people’s rage. And I was very angry,” she said, recounting her feelings about the 2020 election, which she falsely maintains was stolen from Trump despite all evidence to the contrary.

She said her change in perspective had been gradual as she started to see podcasters like Tucker Carlson “turn on President Trump” while having their rhetoric amplified by Russian sources.

Loomer, who casts herself as an independent journalist, told the AP she believed her reversal was already changing minds within Trump’s “Make America Great Again” movement.

“Oh, 100%,” she said. “I’ve received messages all day from different people and media and politics and people just who follow me online who said, ’Wow, I didn’t realize how much we’ve been lied to.’ ‘Wow you really opened my eyes.’”

Ukrainian officials seemed to recognize the opportunity of winning over an ardent Trump ally with a large online following. In addition to her interview with Zelenskyy, Loomer had audiences with top Ukrainian officials and the country’s chief rabbi.

“It takes courage to come to Ukraine and not be deterred by Russian propaganda or air raid sirens,” Zelenskyy’s office wrote on social media.

Loomer also got a tour of Dormition Cathedral of Kyiv-Pechersk Lavra, a monastic complex that came under Russian attack last month.

“Laura is very powerful and she’s a very authoritative in the U.S., so I hope that everything she has seen by her own eyes will help her to spread the truth when she is back at the U.S.,” Tetyana Berezhna, the deputy prime minister and Ukrainian minister of culture told the AP. “I do really hope and I believe that her visit will have a huge impact on relations with the U.S. administration.”

While some have tried to downplay Loomer’s influence with the president, he has often followed her advice. She occasionally traveled with him during the 2024 campaign, and last year he purged his National Security Council staff after she raised concerns about their loyalty in an Oval Office meeting.

Trump appears to be tracking Loomer’s trip, sharing video of her conversation with Zelenskyy on social media.

“Very good!!!” he wrote on Thursday evening.

Loomer has a long history of spreading conspiracy theories. She once shared a video that called 9/11 an “inside job” and amplified a lie about Haitian immigrants eating dogs and cats in Ohio, which Trump went on to repeat during a presidential debate with Kamala Harris.

Although Loomer may have changed her mind about Russia’s invasion, her bigoted views have not budged.

“One thing I really love about Ukraine is I haven’t seen a single Muslim here,” she posted on Saturday. “It’s so refreshing.”

But in the interview, she bemoaned how influential podcasters can spread misinformation.

“They have been able to warp people’s minds to the point where people aren’t even capable of analyzing a subject with common sense anymore because they want to depend on these personalities to give them the opinion that they think they should have,” she said, calling the situation “a major national security threat.”

She said she thinks that “information war” has “the potential to be more destructive than any kinetic war that our country may ever face” and called on the Trump administration to take the threat of Russian propaganda, foreign interference and influence operations more seriously.

“I think that some of our leaders are being influenced by propaganda,” she said.

The White House has routinely downplayed the role of Moscow’s influence, especially because Trump has long chaffed at investigations showing that Russia worked to boost his 2016 candidacy.

Loomer has said repeatedly that Ukraine did not finance her trip and insisted she had traveled in her own capacity.

“I can guarantee you I wasn’t paid by anybody. I certainly wasn’t paid by the government of Ukraine to come here,” she said.

“If it’s fake, why did I risk my life? I’m in a bomb shelter right now. I barely slept this week,” she said.
news.summary: “You don’t need to listen to a podcaster and let them influence your opinion about a country. You can look at those facts yourself.”
