news.title: 'Deeply Appalled': Katy Perry Slams White House for Weaponising 'Firework' in Iran Attack Video
news.text: Katy Perry has criticised the White House after it used her hit song Firework in a TikTok video featuring footage of US military strikes on Iran, saying she was never asked for permission and condemning what she described as the use of a song written to inspire hope alongside footage of military action.The singer said she was 'deeply appalled and angry' after the official White House TikTok account posted the video, which paired footage of the strikes with Firework and the caption, 'Iran has been warned.' Perry said she neither approved nor supported the video's use of the song, arguing that it contradicted the message she intended when writing it.The dispute marks the latest clash between artists and the Trump administration over the political use of music and other creative works, echoing previous objections by musicians whose work has been used in political campaigns or government messaging without their endorsement.Perry Says Song's Message Was DistortedPerry responded publicly on X after the White House video circulated online.'I am deeply appalled and angry to see "Firework" used on the @WhiteHouse TikTok account as a backing track for video footage of military strikes,' she wrote. 'I did not approve this, I was not asked, and I absolutely do not condone it.'She said she wrote Firework 'to be an anthem of hope, healing, and inner strength for people going through their darkest personal moments.''To see a message of self-worth and upliftment used to soundtrack destruction and violence is a complete violation of everything my song stands for,' Perry added.Perry's statement focused on what she described as the contrast between the song's intended message and the way it was presented in the White House video.White House Video Draws AttentionThe White House's TikTok post synchronised the lyric 'boom, boom, boom' with footage of military strikes while displaying the message, 'Iran has been warned.'The video quickly spread across social media, prompting debate over both the choice of music and the administration's presentation of the military operation.At the time of writing, the White House had not publicly responded to Perry's criticism or explained why Firework was selected for the video.It is also unclear under what licensing arrangement, if any, the song was used.Latest Clash Over Political Use Of MusicPerry is far from the first artist to object to the Trump administration's use of creative works.In recent months, Olivia Rodrigo and Sabrina Carpenter have criticised the administration over the use of their material in official social media posts. Children's publisher Kids Can Press also objected after characters from its Franklin the Turtle books appeared in White House content without endorsement.The dispute follows years of similar complaints involving Trump's political campaigns. Bruce Springsteen, Neil Young, Adele, Rihanna, Pharrell Williams, the Rolling Stones and the estate of Tom Petty have all publicly objected to the use of their music at campaign rallies or political events, with several artists demanding that their songs no longer be played.Although the legal position can vary depending on licensing agreements and the circumstances of each performance or broadcast, legal experts have noted that artists may still object if the use creates the impression of endorsement or conflicts with the intended message of their work.Perry's Response Reflects Long-Held ViewsPerry has long been active in Democratic politics, publicly supporting Hillary Clinton in 2016, Joe Biden in 2020 and Kamala Harris during the 2024 presidential campaign.However, her response to the White House video focused primarily on the purpose of Firework rather than her broader political views. Throughout her statement, she described the song as one intended to promote hope, self-belief and personal resilience, values she said were incompatible with imagery of military strikes.Debate Extends Beyond One SongThe incident has renewed discussion about how popular music is used in political communication and whether artists should have greater control over those associations.For Perry, the issue was not simply that Firework appeared in an official government video. She said her objection was that a song she wrote to encourage hope and self-worth was used to accompany images of military action, which she believes is inconsistent with its original purpose.At the time of writing, it remains unclear whether the White House will respond to Perry's criticism. The administration has not publicly addressed her statement or indicated whether the video will remain online.
news.author: Chrys Brent Deiparine

(COMMERCIAL BREAK)

MARTHA RADDATZ, ABC “THIS WEEK” CO-ANCHOR: As the war in Iran enters its sixth month, President Trump weighed a major escalation. But that may be off the table for now. This morning, we’re on the ground in Jordan. A special edition of “THIS WEEK” starts right now.

DONALD TRUMP, PRESIDENT OF THE UNITED STATES: We’re locked and loaded and ready to go, but we’re talking to them.

RADDATZ: This morning --

RADDATZ: We speak to Senator Chris Van Hollen about what this mounting cost means for Americans.

The battle for Maine.

TROY JACKSON, (D) MAINE SENATE CANDIDATE: She’s a rubber stamp for Trump, voting 96 percent of the time with him.

SEN. SUSAN COLLINS, (R) MAINE: He’s a Bernie bro.

CAROL ACEVEDO, MOTHER OF SGT. ANGEL RAMPERSAD: My daughter was a good -- a good soldier.

(END VIDEO CLIP)

ANNOUNCER: From ABC News, a special edition of "This Week." Reporting live from Jordan, Martha Raddatz.

RADDATZ: Good morning from Amman, Jordan.

We have been here since first getting word that three young American soldiers were killed in an Iranian drone and missile strike more than a week ago. A fourth soldier lost his life in Iraq. The three killed here and many more injured were attacked during the night. We don’t know the exact circumstances. We do know that prefabricated housing units, where our service members sleep, were targeted and destroyed in the Iranian strike.

President Trump was there when the remains of the fallen were brought back to the U.S. Their deaths bring the number of service members killed in this war to 18.

It’s easy to forget, looking at official military photos, that these service members were daughters and sons, fathers, mothers, husbands, wives, brothers and sisters.

And while the president offered kind words and comfort to the families, at the same time he appeared to downplay the death toll, on social media comparing the number to other wars. The president, who campaigned as the candidate who would get us out of wars, also defensive about the fact that this war, his war, is soon entering its sixth month, after he predicted it would be over in a matter of weeks.

Another chart he posted on social media comparing this war with the lengthy conflicts in Iraq and Afghanistan. Indeed, so far it has been far shorter.

But those lengthy wars began much like this one, with promises of a swift result, a cakewalk in the case of Iraq. We all remember that.

It is easy to be numb to all of this with the nightly exchange of missiles with Iran. But we shouldn’t be. This is one of the most consequential weeks of this conflict. Oil prices spiking once again. The Red Sea now compromised. And this morning, after threatening a new massive strike and then reportedly taking that off the table for now, the strategy to end this war is still unclear, even after those deadly attacks on Americans.

(BEGIN VIDEOTAPE)

RADDATZ (voice over): This was the moment of impact. Fiery explosions from deadly Iranian missiles and drones at the U.S. base here in Jordan. The attacks soon spreading to American bases across the region, prompting President Trump to consider a massive escalation.

DONALD TRUMP, PRESIDENT OF THE UNITED STATES: We’re locked and loaded and ready to go.

And the Iranians notice all of this, Martha, and they're not going to take him seriously. And that has got to be incredibly frustrating to a president who all he cares about is that people take him seriously.

RADDATZ: And I want to go to you, Donna, on this. I have a feeling you agree with some of that, but I want to talk about the budget request on Capitol Hill, $67 billion. The Democrats pushed back and pushed back hard, but you heard what Pete Hegseth said, look, this just shows you don't support the troops.

That is some -- the troops, rather. That's something they're going to hear again and again.

DONNA BRAZILE, FORMER DNC CHAIR & ABC NEWS CONTRIBUTOR: Well, Martha, as you all know, the Democrats do support our service members, both who have been wounded, and, of course, the 18 service members have been killed. We also need to hear from the Department of Veteran Affairs so that we can support those troops once they're back home.

The bottom line is, without a strategy, without an off-ramp, and with the negotiators probably somewhere between Mar-a-Lago and Switzerland, we need to understand what is the next step. We haven't heard of any escalation over the last 48 hours. Somehow or another, the strikes have stopped.

But will the team get back together to put together the memorandum of understanding so that there can be a real ceasefire and negotiations can continue to end this war?

RADDATZ: Mary, I want to talk about that Saudi deal. You heard me talking about that earlier. But how did that happen, that that was signed and then, oh, wait a minute, it's not actually as we told you it was?

BRUCE: Yeah. It's pretty astounding. I mean, Energy Secretary, Chris Wright and his Saudi counterpart signed this deal, this civilian nuclear agreement. And then, of course, just 24 hours later, after the president announced this, he puts in place this new condition that really puts the entire deal at jeopardy, now insisting that Saudi Arabia has to join the Abraham Accords, of course, that would require them to normalize relations with Israel, something that they've said won't happen unless Israel agrees to a Palestinian state.

So it is highly unlikely to see how this is going to go forward. Certainly, the president can put the brakes on it now as he goes back and forth with the Saudis about this condition. But the White House, after the deal was announced and signed, made it very clear that unless they join the Abraham Accords, there will be no deal, Martha.

RADDATZ: Chris, I want to turn back to the midterms. A lot can happen in 100 days, but this escalation has meant a hit on the economy again. The White House, Republicans truly have to be worried about what happens. That is all the people care about. They don't like the way this war is being handled, and they don't like what's happening to the economy. So what do Republicans do?

CHRISTIE: Well, Martha, look, Republicans, my party, has got to be scared, and especially some very good members of Congress who otherwise might deserve re-election are weighed down by the following.

Look at the numbers in the Fox News poll last week. The president's job approval is at 38.61 percent. But worse, he's 34 points underwater on the economy, 32 points underwater on Iran. And the bigger problem in these swing districts for the House and these swing states in the Senate is what's going on with Independents.

The president's job approval is 41 points underwater with Independents, and he's 66 points underwater on inflation with Independents. Those are deadly numbers.

And so, you know, for Republicans, they're going to have to start making a decision. Do they try to distance themselves from this president? And this is going to be the first time he's going to have to confront that potentially. Either they're going to go down with him as he's going down. And these are Fox News poll numbers.

So you know, we got some real problems as a party, and it's going to affect those with Republican governors this past week. And there's a lot of Republican gubernatorial races that we are very, very worried about in states that we have always won. And that's a real problem.

RADDATZ: And Donna, let's talk about the Senate, particularly Maine. We've also got Michigan. Graham Platner replaced, he was a prominent -- Troy Jackson was a prominent Platner supporter, but he also came in third place in Maine's gubernatorial primary. So how confident are you that Troy Jackson could beat Susan Collins?

BRAZILE: I'm very confident. Look, he's a logger. He's somebody who has been around the state of Maine for a long time. I believe he can put together the electoral coalition that will win in the state of Maine. He knows that state very well. He knows how to connect with working people.

And I think Mr. Jackson is going to prove to be a very competitive candidate. I know he has 100 days, but the people of Maine are very motivated, and you saw that in the convention.

In terms of Michigan, their primary is coming up next week, I mean, on August 4th. That is also a very competitive state. You have a mainstream Democrat running against an insurgent or, what we like to call, a very energetic candidate from the left. That's going to also be a state that we need to win.

But Democrats also have another path. We've got Alaska that's still in play, Iowa that's still in play. And if we keep Georgia and we can improve in North Carolina, Democrats are still competitive in the United States Senate as well as the House.

Look, Democrats have a great deal of momentum right now. We've won 90 percent of the races since Trump's been in office. I'm confident that we can take back the Congress.

CHRISTIE: Martha, let me just say, and remind my friend, Donna, that the road is littered with the people who are going to beat Susan Collins. And so, I would feel very nervous about Maine with 100 days and an unproven statewide candidate against one of the most able political actors this town has seen over the last 30 years.

RADDATZ: And Mary, I want to go to you about Mikie Sherrill, Chris' state's governor. She announced that about 6,600 non-citizens were mistakenly registered to vote because of a technical error a few years ago. They didn't try to pretend they were citizens, but she said less than 400 actually voted, and there's no evidence of them swaying elections.

But this becomes a PR nightmare and a really strong narrative going forward about election security.

BRUCE: Yes. And the president, no surprise, was very quick to pounce on this, saying that it just underscores his desire to pass the SAVE America Act, that voting legislation that he's been pushing that would require voter I.D. and proof of citizenship. And Governor Sherrill, you know, tried to come out and be as transparent as she could about this. She said when they find problems, they fix them.

But, you know, she said it was this computer error that went over 6,000 people went to sign up to get a driver's license that they were erroneously also signed up and registered to vote. Now, she said and stressed that while about 400 of them did go on to actually vote, that there's no evidence that any of those votes were able to sway elections, but certainly the president believes that this adds fuel to his fire as he's been amping up those unproven claims of widespread voter fraud.

CHRISTIE: Martha, let me give you one thing. The governor has appointed my former attorney general, very independent, Jeff Chiesa, to do a bipartisan investigation. Look for that because he will not hide anything from the public. You can count on it.

BRAZILE: Good.

RADDATZ: OK. Thanks to all of you. Appreciate your time.

Up next, we remember the service members who made the ultimate sacrifice in this war. We'll be right back.

(COMMERCIAL BREAK)

RADDATZ: President Trump at the dignified transfer of the four fallen soldiers killed in Iraq and Jordan this week, leaving the families with the realities of sacrifice and hopefully leaving all of us with gratitude for their willingness to serve.

(BEGIN VIDEOTAPE)

RADDATZ (voice-over): There were two young women, a father and a beloved son, engaged to be married. The three Americans killed here in Jordan, all under 30, now posthumously promoted. Staff Sergeant Angel Rampersad, 28, of Ozone Park, New York. Captain Tyler Finn, 25, of Ewa Beach, Hawaii, and the youngest at just 19 years old Private 1st Class Isabella Gonzalez of Carrollton, Texas.

Staff Sergeant Michael Swinton was from Fayetteville, North Carolina. He was killed at a U.S. base in Iraq when an Iranian drone exploded in a controlled detonation.

He was 30. Their remains arriving on U.S. soil on the same aircraft, casualties of the same conflict. The families of these men and women grieving, heartbroken, yet filled with pride.

CAROL ACEVEDO, MOTHER OF STAFF SGT. ANGEL RAMPERSAD: My daughter was a good soldier. She fought for this country and she died for this country. And I am a mother who is highly proud of her.

RADDATZ (voice-over): Carol Acevedo's daughter, Angel Sarah Rampersad, was born in Trinidad. Her mother brought her to the U.S. when she was just a baby. Her mom insisted she go to college before signing up for the military. A few days after her 21st birthday, she enlisted in the army. There, she met the woman who would become her wife.

Isabella Gonzales, the 19-year-old, joined just after graduating from high school. In her native Texas, pain rippling through the community.

JOHN NORSWORTHY, AMERICAN LEGION POST 597 COMMANDER: I've been interviewed today several times. And they always ask me, why does it mean so much? It just does. Everybody that served knew that could have been him. They would have been right there next to her.

RADDATZ (voice-over): Staff Sgt. Michael Swinton was the father of a six-year-old boy and a four-year-old girl. His wife, Mia, who he met in the army, told us he was an amazing husband and father.

Captain Tyler Feehan was an officer who served in the ROTC at Southern Utah University with plans for law school after his army service, and plans to marry his fiance when he returned home. His fiance, Claire, writing that Tyler poured his heart into serving those under his leadership.

Every day, he would come home and tell me stories about his soldiers. He believed that leadership began with kindness, humility, and genuinely caring about people. The parents of the avid hiker writing online, "Tyler, we are proud of you beyond words. Devastated, yes, but prouder still."

You can see Feehan here when he was commissioned as an officer in the army, saluting his grandfather. His family tells us this image is especially powerful now. Tyler's grandfather died on Thursday, five days after his grandson was killed. The Feehan family telling us the two of them are now together again.

(END VIDEOTAPE)

RADDATZ (on camera): We grieve with those families and send respect and prayers. We'll be right back.

(COMMERCIAL BREAK)

RADDATZ: That's all for us today from Amman, Jordan. Thanks for sharing part of your Sunday with us. Check out "World News Tonight" and have a great day.

(COMMERCIAL BREAK)

news.title: House Republicans ‘in the strongest position’ ever 100 days from midterms: Memo
news.text:
The committee outlines a number of positions of strength, including a fundraising advantage it has over its Democratic counterpart. The memo says the NRCC has a $13.7 million dollar advantage over the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee, putting the NRCC in the “strongest cash position” in 20 years. It also mentions the Supreme Court’s recent decision striking down the limits on spending individual candidates could do in conjunction with party committees, meaning “airtime, staff, and turnout operations are locked in across every district.”

House Republican fundraisers also argue that the battlefield favors them. “Democrats are defending 23 seats President Trump won in 2024,” compared to eight Republicans running in seats that former Vice President Kamala Harris carried. The national map was greatly influenced by a flurry of redistricting pursuits across the country this cycle. Republicans emerged with a narrow advantage: Trump would have carried 14 of the remapped seats by at least 10 points.

“To flip the House, Democrats have to win Republican-held seats where President Trump averaged 53.2% in 2024. That’s a much tougher battlefield than 2018, when Democrats flipped seats, averaging just 46.6% for President Trump in 2016,” the memo reads.

The NRCC highlights five critical districts it hopes to flip: Maine’s 2nd District, where Rep. Jared Golden (D-ME) is retiring; North Carolina’s 1st District, a redistricted seat held by Rep. Don Davis (D-NC); New Mexico’s 2nd District, a southern New Mexico seat held by Rep. Gabe Vasquez (D-NM); Texas’s 34th District, represented by Rep. Vicente Gonzales (D-TX) in the Rio Grande Valley; and Washington’s 3rd District, a Republican-leaning seat flipped by Rep. Marie Gluesenkamp Perez (D-WA) in 2022.

Public opinion has also given Republicans reason for optimism. Democrats’ generic ballot polling advantage has shrunk from over 7 points to about 5 points in the last month. Moreover, Republicans are emboldened by the Democratic Party’s low approval rating, with some surveys showing the party’s favorability at historic lows, and the party’s nomination of “socialist” candidates, which could cost Democrats in critical toss-up seats.

HOUSE STARTS ITS AUGUST RECESS AND KICKS OFF CRUCIAL CAMPAIGN STRETCH

Republicans do face a series of headwinds in order to maintain the majority. The last time the party in the White House gained seats in the midterms was in 2002, when Republicans gained eight seats. Republicans lost 41 seats during Trump’s first midterm in 2018. Democrats lost nine seats in 2022. Trump’s approval rating, in which he’s 23 points underwater, according to the Economist, the lowest mark of his second term, may also pose a political obstacle for Republicans as midterm elections are typically referenda on the president.

“The next 100 days won’t be easy; they’ll be a knife fight. Democrats will spend millions trying to claw back the majority. But campaigns aren’t won through wishful thinking,” the memo concludes.

news.title: Which Way Should the Democratic Party Go Now?
news.text:
The fast-approaching 2026 midterm elections present the Democrats with both an opportunity and a crisis. The opportunity exists because President Donald Trump is unpopular, has failed to stop the rise in consumer prices that helped doom his predecessor, and seems unable to end the aimless war in Iran that he started. Americans now tell pollsters that they are more likely to vote for Democrats than for Republicans this fall. The crisis is that a narrow victory may not be sufficient to dislodge Trumpism, which is now deeply entrenched in government. And, though the Democratic leadership is looking to recapture the resistance spirit of 2018, its defining problem is a long-standing one in the Party of how to manage the movement that Senator Bernie Sanders started a decade ago, whose populist appeal and generational momentum it needs in this anti-institutional moment but whose principles it does not fully share.
That tension has been most vividly on view in Maine, where the Republican senator Susan Collins is now seeking a sixth term in a state that Kamala Harris won by more than six points in 2024. Platner’s emergence there last year had the quality of myth. A couple of left-wing political operatives saw Platner, an oyster farmer, in a local video opposing the development of a corporate salmon farm in Frenchman Bay, and matched his name to records of donors to Sanders’s campaigns. Platner, they learned, was also a harbormaster and a veteran of two Marine combat tours in Iraq and an Army tour in Afghanistan. One of the operatives reportedly e-mailed colleagues that Platner was “one of the most talented politicians of our time. Maybe any time”; both Sanders and Senator Elizabeth Warren endorsed him. He did turn out to be a commanding barnstormer, a foul-mouthed and fluent denouncer of wealth and corruption, whose appeal drove the sitting governor of Maine, Janet Mills, out of the race. But his candidacy collapsed in a series of scandals, involving first a Nazi-associated tattoo and offensive posts, then allegations of bad behavior toward women, and, finally, untenably, an accusation of rape. Platner denied it, but he dropped out.
One theory heard often in politics is that the Democrats are repeating, in ideological inverse, the experience of the Republicans in 2010, when the Tea Party overtook the G.O.P., eventually clearing the way for Trump. (“Warning for Democrats’ Future Is Lurking in GOP’s Past,” a USA Today headline put it, with impressive concision.) Such takes refer to a parallel not just in the rise of populists like Platner but also in primary upsets of powerful incumbents by radical newcomers affiliated with the Democratic Socialists of America. The chair of the Congressional Hispanic Caucus, Representative Adriano Espaillat, of New York City, and Representative Diana DeGette, of Denver, a progressive stalwart, were defeated by young insurgents, Darializa Avila Chevalier and Melat Kiros, respectively, who came out of the Gaza protest movement and the D.S.A., and who took some positions far outside the mainstream. (During an interview with the online publication The New York Editorial Board, Chevalier declined to specify whether her support of prison abolition meant that a man who randomly killed another man should not be sent to prison.) A columnist for The Atlantic wrote, “The D.S.A. is a parasite.”
That reaction perhaps suggests that there have been more of these upsets than is the case. In races where an incumbent congressional Democrat has lost this year, anger over Gaza has played a role, and in each of them the issue has drawn both donations and attention. But across the country only five Democratic incumbents have lost primaries—two of them because of redistricting—which does not really add up to a revolution. An alternative theory to the Tea Party one is that the general sense of emergency in 2026 has led Democrats, and especially the rising young figures hoping to lead the Party, to embrace political pragmatism.
This summer, two politicians have caught the attention of the Party’s base, both of whom are under forty. On the left, Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, of New York, pointedly declined to endorse Platner—even before the rape accusation, she called the mounting claims against him “hard to stomach”—and has been favorably cited by David Axelrod, Barack Obama’s political guru, for echoing the former President’s themes of hope and change. From the center, Jon Ossoff, running for reëlection to the Senate in Georgia, spoke critically of the Gaza war early on, and has focussed a controlled campaign on the President’s corruption, a traditional populist theme. These approaches seem to be working: in an Emerson 2028 Presidential-primary poll, Ocasio-Cortez and Ossoff were tied for third place, just behind Pete Buttigieg and Gavin Newsom.
Such political talent is rare. In Maine, to replace Platner, the Democrats eventually settled on Troy Jackson, the most organized of the prospects. A former logger who finished third in this year’s gubernatorial primary, Jackson lacked Platner’s ability to excite the public, but he was preferred by supporters of Sanders, who had endorsed him for governor.(Collins called Jackson a “Bernie bro.”) And, having spent six years as the president of the state Senate, he was palatable to the Party establishment. Last week, Jackson tweeted that Collins had “helped destroy Roe v. Wade, she advanced Trump’s $990 billion Medicaid cuts, and she gave ICE $70 billion to continue its rogue terror campaigns.” Political pabulum, yes, but maybe also a preview of what the Democrats’ campaigns this fall will offer: not exactly transformation, not even resolution, just a dogged and prosaic insistence that things in the country are going very badly. ♦
news.summary: It’s been a tumultuous primary season, but is this the Democrats’ Tea Party moment? Or is something more pragmatic emerging?
news.author: Benjamin Wallace-Wells

news.title: Maine Democrats made the right choice with Troy Jackson
news.text:
Maine Democrats on Saturday selected former Maine Senate President Troy Jackson to replace Graham Platner as the party’s U.S. Senate nominee. Jackson now has just three months to make his case that Mainers should pick him to represent them in Washington over five-term Republican Sen. Susan Collins. 

The Democrats’ scramble echoes the 2024 presidential election, when Kamala Harris ran for president after President Joe Biden withdrew. In this case, Jackson is the one taking the reins toward the end of a tight high-stakes race after his predecessor imploded and dropped out. But considering the disastrous circumstances, the nomination of Jackson looks like a pretty decent outcome for Democrats. There’s reason for cautious optimism that he could prevail in his race, given his unique position as a progressive insider with something to offer voters looking for populist outsiders.

This may end up being the smoothest passing of the baton Democrats could have hoped for.

It all came together shockingly fast. Platner’s campaign collapsed after a sexual assault allegation, and Democrats had less than two weeks to figure out how to replace him on the ballot. And the outcome of the convention held on Saturday had, in fact, been determined by the quickly cobbled-together process leading up to it. 

The week before the state convention, registered Democrats voted in county-level mini-conventions in which they selected delegates to send to the state convention. The process was rushed and ad hoc, and the participation in the state conventions was less than a tenth of the primary, but the results were clear: Jackson dominated, winning 478 of 500 delegates up for grabs. Saturday’s state convention was a mere formality. 

This may end up being the smoothest passing of the baton Democrats could have hoped for. At the level of state politics, Jackson is understood to be a logical replacement for Platner: He campaigned with him before his scandals, and according to Slate, he had the support of about 75% of the volunteers who had rallied behind Platner.

Jackson, 58, is a known quantity in Maine, having worked for over two decades in state politics, including both in the state Senate and in the state House of Representatives. He has the trust of the state party establishment and has a good reputation among progressive groups in the state. The power of his reputation was evident during the rapid-fire nomination process, as Jackson was able to secure the rapid backing of unions in the state and quickly rack up delegates. “Troy’s been around,” Jason Shedlock, a labor leader in Maine, told CNN. “If you don’t know him, you know somebody who does. And if you don’t know somebody who does, the person standing next to them has been impacted by him.”

At the same time, Jackson has progressive credentials that mirror much of Platner’s policy platform and will help him claim populist status. Before he got into politics, Jackson was a fifth-generation logger and participated in high-profile labor activism. He has supported progressive policies, and his unsuccessful campaign for governor this year was backed by Sen. Bernie Sanders of Vermont. Jackson’s policy platform for Senate includes demands for Medicare for All, taxing billionaires, abolishing Immigration and Customs Enforcement and cutting off aid to Israel’s military to “end the genocide in Gaza.” He said he doesn’t support Sen. Chuck Schumer of New York to continue as leader of the Senate Democrats. (He said he prefers Sanders.) Maine Democrats who were excited by Platner’s platform and voted for him overwhelmingly in the primary have little reason to recoil from Jackson.

Jackson also exhibits shades of Platner in one other way: a history of reactionary views. Jackson started in Maine politics as a Republican and entered the Maine State House as an independent, before becoming a Democrat in 2004. He used to be a social conservative, voting against gay marriage and abortion rights. But he has expressed regret about those views, and for years he has supported gay marriage and robust abortion rights, and has since gained the strong backing of advocacy groups that support those rights. His campaign platform calls for a federal right to abortion. Depending on one’s perspective, Jackson’s political evolution could be an asset or a liability. At worst, he could be slammed as unreliable and a chameleon. At best, he will be seen as independent-minded and willing to learn from mistakes. 

Jackson currently occupies a competitive position in the polls. A University of New Hampshire poll of likely general election voters in Maine conducted between July 15 and July 20 — that is, while Jackson was gaining momentum before the convention — found 49% of respondents said they would vote for him if the election were held today, while 46% said they would vote for Collins. Meanwhile, 2% said “another candidate” and 3% said they were undecided. And in a promising sign of momentum, even before he clinched the nomination, Jackson raised $1 million for his Senate bid. That’s a lot for a guy who barely raised more than that over the course of an entire campaign for governor, which lasted about a year.

We don’t know if Jackson will maintain such a competitive position against a longtime incumbent. He doesn’t have Platner’s charisma, and his weaknesses are about to be tested. But the buzz that Platner generated is lingering around this race, and Maine is considered a must-win if Democrats are to win back the Senate. Jackson has a decent combination of qualities going for him, as a politician with experience and trust across the state and with a vision that will not betray the many Mainers who were enthralled with Platner before his fall from grace.
news.author: Ja’han Jones

news.title: Will the US and Canada be friends again?
news.text:
How did this all begin?

We can trace the origins back to one of Trump’s social media posts. He had just defeated then-Vice President Kamala Harris in the 2024 election, and was gearing up for his second term in the Oval Office. As part of his forthcoming agenda, Trump announced that Canada and Mexico faced the prospect of significant tariffs.

“On January 20th, as one of my many first Executive Orders, I will sign all necessary documents to charge Mexico and Canada a 25% Tariff on ALL products coming into the United States, and its ridiculous Open Borders,” he wrote on Truth Social on Nov. 25, 2024. “This Tariff will remain in effect until such time as Drugs, in particular Fentanyl, and all Illegal Aliens stop this Invasion of our Country! Both Mexico and Canada have the absolute right and power to easily solve this long simmering problem. We hereby demand that they use this power, and until such time that they do, it is time for them to pay a very big price!”

Trump’s position was understandable. Then-Canadian Prime Minister Justin Trudeau and his Liberal government, who were in power during his first presidential term, had barely focused on North American border safety and security for most of his nine years in office. The black market for illegal weapons and drugs was still a significant problem. Immigration to Canada had skyrocketed to unprecedented and unaffordable levels, with serious concerns about a faulty vetting process and illegal aliens having remained largely unaddressed.

It’s no secret that Trump doesn’t respect weak, ineffective political leaders. It’s also no secret that Trudeau was one of the worst of this miserable lot. He’s a left-wing mediocrity enamored with political correctness, environmentalism, and gender consciousness. He spent the taxpayers’ money like a drunken sailor, had no political backbone, didn’t understand economics (he once bizarrely said the Canadian budget “will balance itself” in a Feb. 2014 television interview, and told reporters in Aug. 2021, “you’ll forgive me if I don’t think about monetary policy”), made off-the-wall remarks like “peoplekind” in public with a straight face, and preferred soft, squishy negotiations with public figures. That’s why Trump described Trudeau as “meek and mild” and “very dishonest and weak,” during the G7 meetings in June 2018, among many other vivid descriptions.

Trump likely didn’t want to face the prospect of dealing with Trudeau’s left-wing, out-of-touch nonsense once more. He found a way to get rid of him, whether by accident or design. Fox News reported that during a Nov. 29, 2024, dinner meeting at Mar-a-Lago, Trudeau told Trump the tariffs would “kill the Canadian economy completely.” Trump responded, “So, your country can’t survive unless it’s ripping off the U.S. to the tune of $100 billion?” He followed up with an amusing proposal: Canada could “become the 51st state.” While Trump acknowledged to Trudeau that “prime minister is a better title,” he could still be “governor of the 51st state.” The president-elect clearly enjoyed getting under Trudeau’s skin with jokes, quips, and memes about this meeting. While the PM’s popularity numbers were already crumbling at this point, this controversy played a major role in his decision to resign in January 2025.

Yet, it’s been clear since the beginning that Trump wasn’t being serious. If Canada ever wanted to willingly join the U.S., he would have welcomed these discussions like any U.S. president would. The White House was surely aware of polling data that consistently showed Canada overwhelmingly had no interest in pursuing this. And while Trump never had any plans of annexing Canada or using military force, a January 2025 Angus Reid poll revealed that 62% of respondents didn’t trust him.

That’s why Trump used this situation to his personal and political advantage not only with Trudeau, but also with his successor, Mark Carney.

The former governor of the Bank of Canada and Bank of England is a different political foe — and a more intelligent, competent individual. This didn’t trouble the president in any way, shape or form. Why? Carney had no political experience and didn’t understand the dog-eat-dog world of politics.

As I wrote in a May 1, 2025 National Post column, he was “socially awkward, aloof, egotistical and doesn’t possess a backbone.” I also pointed out in a March 16, 2025, National Post column that Carney and Trudeau weren’t that dissimilar. “They’re both left-wing, pro-government intervention, distrusting of privatization and free markets, favourable towards wealth redistribution, supportive of radical environmentalist policies, woke ideology and political correctness — and more.” 

Trump, therefore, decided to help keep Carney in office by interjecting himself into the April 28, 2025, Canadian election. This was accomplished in several strategic ways.

The U.S.-Canada tariff war intensified during the campaign and became the main political issue for Canada’s electorate. Right-leaning provincial premiers like Ontario’s Doug Ford and Alberta’s Danielle Smith both intervened with the Trump White House, albeit in different ways and with different degrees of success. Carney’s moronic “elbows up” campaign to combat Trump and tariffs was successful for a spell, too. The president’s political agenda was top of mind for Canadian voters, while everything else became secondary or irrelevant.

Canada needed a white knight to take on Trump. This role could have been assumed by Conservative leader Pierre Poilievre. He had led Trudeau’s Liberals for over two years in the polls, and his lead had stretched out to more than 20 points. But while many Canadian progressives incorrectly believed that Trump and Poilievre were two sides of the same political coin — nothing could have been further from the truth, since Poilievre firmly believed in free markets, free trade, and more personal liberties and freedoms — the former wanted nothing to do with the latter.

“I think his biggest problem is he’s not a MAGA guy, you know? I mean, he’s really not… a Trump guy at all,” Trump said during a Feb. 28, 2025, interview with The Spectator’s Ben Domenech. Trump also told Fox News’s Laura Ingraham on Mar. 19, 2025, that Poilievre is “stupidly no friend of mine” and “I think it’s easier to deal actually with a Liberal.”

That last line was quite revealing. Trump wanted Carney, not Poilievre, at the other end of the bargaining table. He was going to do everything in his power to achieve it.

A Canadian readout of the first Carney-Trump phone call on Mar. 28, 2025, suggested the two leaders had had a “constructive conversation” and “agreed to begin comprehensive negotiations about a new economic and security relationship immediately following the election.” A March 30, 2025, Ipsos poll showed Carney leading Poilievre in categories like “someone who is best to manage during tough economic times” and “someone who is best to represent Canada on the world stage,” and had a surprising 12-point lead as the best leader who could “stand up to President Trump.” There wasn’t a shred of evidence to prove this, but many Canadians were too blind with rage and anti-American sentiment to realize what the president was doing, and did, to keep Carney as prime minister.

Carney was determined to repair Canada-U.S. relations at first, including stronger stances on border security, illegal immigration, and fentanyl. This position has slowed down considerably. He went from Canada being in “intensive negotiations with the Americans” to end tariffs last June, to “nothing’s assured” and Canada will only accept the “right deal” a couple of weeks later, to cryptic attacks against Trump in his Davos speech in January about a “rupture in the world order,” “gaps between rhetoric and reality” and “American hegemony.” Carney also released a short video in April that led some analysts suggested was a nod to FDR’s fireside chats. In reality, it was more of a soapbox to push back against Trump without naming him directly. To wit, “We can’t control the disruption coming from our neighbors. We can’t bet our future on the hope that it will suddenly stop. But we can control what happens here.”

The PM’s current strategy has been to diversify Canada’s political, economic, and military interests. He’s built closer ties between Canada and the European Union, suggesting the former was the “most European of non-European countries.” He’s also increased trade relations with other countries, including a controversial “strategic partnership” with China. While political and economic diversification is perfectly fine, Carney is doing this at the expense of the badly damaged Canada-U.S. relationship.

Carney’s new direction has impacted the U.S.-Mexico-Canada Agreement, too. Trump had recently told reporters, “I’m not looking to renew it… We don’t need anything to Canada has, we don’t need anything that Mexico has, but they need everything that we have, and they have to treat us better.”

While the president had made similar nonchalant remarks about this trade deal (including when it was still known as the North American Free Trade Agreement) and the renegotiation process, it had never been quite this direct. The White House ultimately decided against renewing it on July 1. The USMCA will now enter a period of annual review until it expires on July 1, 2036, or one of the three countries gives a six-month advance notice of a formal withdrawal. Did Carney’s decision to thumb his nose at Trump play a role in this? It’s certainly possible.

There’s also the Pentagon’s recent decision to pause its participation in the Permanent Joint Board of Defense, which Canada and the U.S. established on Aug. 17, 1940. The Brian Mulroney Institute for Government noted that it “helped provide a framework for continental defence cooperation between Canada and the United States during the Second World War.” The PJBD evolved into a “senior advisory body on continental security for Canada and the United States” after the war ended, as well as a “forum for Canadian and American diplomatic and military leaders to handle politically sensitive matters.” There have been some prominent board members, including former New York City mayor Fiorello H. La Guardia. U.S. military representatives “were placed under the Joint Chiefs of Staff” by December 1947. The PJBP has been involved in NORAD, Distant Early Warning System, Airborne Warning & Control System, the Alaska Highway, and the St. Lawrence Seaway.

Undersecretary of War Elbridge Colby posted on social media that this decision was made because “Canada has failed to make credible progress on its defense commitments.” Colby said the Department of War would “reassess how this forum benefits shared North American defense… We can no longer avoid the gaps between rhetoric and reality. Real powers must sustain our rhetoric with shared defense and security responsibilities.”

How did Carney and Canada respond to this serious dressing-down by Colby and the Pentagon? Not the way you would expect. The PM inexplicably said the PJBD “has a long heritage but I wouldn’t overplay the importance of this. We have many aspects of very close defence co-operation with the United States…There’s lots of co-operation we will continue to do so.”

Really? There may be other components to defense and security matters, but the decision to pause this 86-year-old board was far from insignificant. When a longtime friend and ally suggests you’re not taking safety and security issues seriously enough, you should overplay its importance, period.

Will the U.S. and Canada ever get on the same page again? Yes, but it will take time and effort on the part of both sides.

Ensuring the USMCA’s annual review goes well for the remainder of Trump’s second presidential term should go without saying. An estimated $3.6 billion CAD (roughly $2.6 billion USD) in imports and exports flows through the Canada-U.S. border every day. Trade matters to individuals and businesses in both of our countries, and it needs to be preserved and protected. And who knows? While Trump has never been enthusiastic about NAFTA or the USMCA, maybe he’ll change his mind if Carney modifies his position, language, and tone about looking for new trade partners outside of the U.S.

TRUMP TO IMPOSE 50% TARIFFS ON CANADA IN RESPONSE TO RETALITORY DUTIES 

Carney’s support of the “Fortress North America” concept could be helpful, too. “Canada Strong will help Make America Great Again,” the PM said in a speech to the Economic Club of New York with some Trump-inspired language.“While Canada and the United States have had our differences over the centuries, we have always worked and eventually worked through them because we share values and our common interests run deep.” In the PM’s view, “a fortress North America is in everyone’s interest.” While the fortress is usually discussed in economic terms, it will also cover defense, security, and geopolitical concerns. There’s an opportunity for Carney and Trump to work together to create a secure border, clamp down on illegal immigration, drugs, and crime levels, and prove to the U.S. that safety and security matter to the Canadian government.

Canada and the U.S. need to become friends once more. It’s up to Carney and Trump to find a way to put their political and personal differences aside and work together to rebuild the broken relationship between our countries. Let’s hope they find a path to success before long.

Michael Taube, a columnist for the National Post, Troy Media, and Loonie Politics, was a speechwriter for former Canadian Prime Minister Stephen Harper.
news.summary: There was a time not too long ago when the relationship between Canada and the United States was positive and nearly impenetrable. Our two countries have been close friends, allies, and trade partners for many years. Canadian and American leaders have obviously had moments of disagreement related to trade, tariffs, border security, declarations of war, […]

news.title: 100 Counties Likely to Decide the 2026 Midterms
news.text: With 100 days left until the midterms on November 3, a Newsweek analysis has identified 100 counties that sit at the center of the battle for Congress. The question of who controls Congress from next year may turn less on broad swing states than on a narrower set of communities: suburban areas where President Donald Trump's 2024 margins were thin, fast-growing metro counties that anchor House battlegrounds, and local political bellwethers that often provide an early indication of where the electorate is moving. Newsweek's analysis combines competitive House battleground districts, Senate battleground states, close 2024 presidential results and recent special-election signals using data from the Cook Political Report, Ballotpedia, BallotWire and Dave Leip’s Atlas of U.S. Presidential Elections. Each category was converted into points, with closer contests and stronger signs of competitiveness generating higher scores. The combined totals were then used to rank the states and districts most likely to be pivotal in the 2026 midterm elections, with some counties emerging repeatedly across multiple battlegrounds. Democratic and Republican campaign committees, Senate candidates and House hopefuls are already targeting many of the places identified in the analysis. A Republican National Committee (RNC) strategist told Newsweek that while Republicans tend to think in terms of congressional districts rather than counties, many of the counties identified in the analysis likely overlap with the districts expected to decide control of the House. “This November will be a choice between communism and common sense,” RNC spokeswoman Delanie Bomar told Newsweek in an emailed statement. “As Democrats lunge further to the Left, and with freedom, public safety, and cost of living on the line, Republicans are on offense and ready to defy history.” The list of all 100 counties seen in the map can be found at the bottom of this article. Use the map below to explore where Newsweek identified as key to the 2026 midterms. The list is not a forecast, but a county-level guide to the places where small shifts in turnout or margins could have national consequences. Maricopa County in Arizona, Northampton County in Pennsylvania, Scott County in Iowa, Eaton County in Michigan and Hidalgo County in Texas all ranked among the strongest candidates to shape the political story of 2026. A Democratic strategist told Newsweek that many of these counties have become increasingly important, saying that they aligned with the party's understanding of the most competitive terrain in the 2026 House battle. And campaign organizations are already drawing up similarly expansive maps. The Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee (DCCC) told Newsweek that it has identified 46 Republican-held seats as its "Districts in Play," while Democratic state legislative strategists say they are tracking hundreds of competitive races nationwide—evidence of how they increasingly view the 2026 battlefield as a contest fought in a relatively small number of communities. The concentration of campaign resources is another reason counties matter. An RNC campaigner told Newsweek that resources are increasingly focused on districts won by narrow margins. The Counties at the Center of the House Battle Few examples are more striking than Maricopa County, Arizona. Trump carried the county by 3.48 percentage points in 2024, making it one of the most closely watched counties in the state. It is also central to multiple competitive House districts around Phoenix, the state's capital and largest city. The open-seat race to replace Republican Representative David Schweikert has emerged as one of the Democrats' top pickup opportunities. Democrat Amish Shah is hoping to capitalize on growing Democratic strength in portions of Maricopa County, while Republican Jay Feely, a former NFL kicker backed by Trump, is seeking to keep the suburban Phoenix-area 1st Congressional District in GOP hands. In Pennsylvania's Lehigh Valley, Northampton County and Lehigh County emerged as two of the strongest candidates in the analysis. Trump carried Northampton by 1.77 points, while former Democratic Vice President Kamala Harris carried neighboring Lehigh by 2.69 points. Both counties sit inside one of the most competitive political districts—Pennsylvania's 7th, where Republican Representative Ryan Mackenzie faces Democrat Bob Brooks, a firefighter union leader and former Bethlehem firefighter—in the country and are likely to attract enormous attention from both parties in 2026. Iowa produced several counties that ranked highly. Trump won Scott County by 3.88 points and Dallas County by 4.72 points. Both counties sit inside competitive House terrain while also belonging to a Senate battleground state. Polk County, home to Des Moines, is less competitive politically but remains one of the state's most important vote-producing counties. Republican Representative Mariannette Miller-Meeks faces Democrat Christina Bohannan in a rematch of one of 2024's closest House races in the country. Bohannan previously came within about 800 votes of unseating Miller-Meeks. Iowa's 1st District includes the Quad Cities area in Scott County. Republican Representative Zach Nunn is defending his seat against Democratic nominee Sarah Trone Garriott, a state senator from West Des Moines, in the 3rd District anchored by Polk County and the fast-growing suburban communities of Dallas County. Michigan's Eaton County also stood out. Trump carried it by just 3.14 points, making it one of the strongest examples of a county that combines House battleground relevance with a narrow presidential margin. Republican Representative Tom Barrett is seeking a second term in one of Michigan's premier battleground districts. The 7th District seat, centered on Lansing and surrounding communities in Ingham and Eaton counties, is expected to be highly competitive. Democrats will choose their nominee in the August 4 primary, with former U.S. Ambassador to Ukraine Bridget Brink, former Navy SEAL Matt Maasdam, and political organizer William Lawrence competing for the place. South Texas featured prominently as well. Trump carried Hidalgo County by 2.87 points and Cameron County by 5.80 points in 2024. In the 15th District, Republican Representative Monica De La Cruz faces Democrat Bobby Pulido, the Tejano music star who won the Democratic nomination and has become one of the party's highest-profile recruits in South Texas. Centered on Hidalgo County, including McAllen and Edinburg, the district sits at the heart of the Rio Grande Valley. Despite the district's Republican lean, analysts have identified Pulido as a potentially strong challenger because of his local name recognition and crossover appeal. Texas' 34th District (Cameron County) sees Democratic Representative Vicente Gonzalez seeking reelection against Republican Eric Flores, a former assistant U.S. attorney and Army National Guard veteran. Senate Battlegrounds Run Through Key Metropolitan Counties The Senate map introduces a different set of counties. Rather than focusing on congressional districts, statewide contests depend heavily on large suburban and metropolitan counties capable of producing hundreds of thousands of votes. Georgia offers one of the clearest examples and is among the Senate battlegrounds identified by Ballotpedia. Democratic Senator Jon Ossoff, the only Democratic Senate incumbent defending a seat in a state won by Trump in 2024, faces Republican Representative Mike Collins. Trump won the state in 2024, but several large counties remain essential to Democratic statewide hopes. Cobb County voted Democratic by 14.88 points, Gwinnett County by 16.51 points and Fulton County by 44.86 points. Together they form a critical part of the Atlanta metropolitan area that often determines statewide outcomes. Michigan presents a similar dynamic. Oakland County voted Democratic by 10.58 points in 2024, while neighboring Macomb County moved in the opposite direction and backed Trump by 13.69 points. Those contrasting political profiles make both counties central to understanding statewide coalition building in Michigan. Michigan is also among the Senate battleground states highlighted by Ballotpedia. With Democratic Senator Gary Peters retiring, Michigan is set to host one of the most competitive Senate races of the 2026 cycle. Republican Mike Rogers, a former congressman and frequent statewide contender, is the GOP's presumptive nominee, while Democrats will choose between Representative Haley Stevens and former public health official Abdul El-Sayed in the August 4 primary. North Carolina's Mecklenburg County, anchored by Charlotte, backed Harris by 32.67 points, while nearby Wake County, home to Raleigh, backed Harris by 25.44 points. Republican candidates often compensate elsewhere in the state, also listed among Senate battlegrounds for 2026, making turnout and margins in both counties crucial metrics on election night. Republican Michael Whatley, the former RNC chairman, faces former Democratic Governor Roy Cooper in one of the most important Senate races of the 2026 cycle. Both candidates cleared their primaries with little difficulty, Nebraska and Maine also produced notable counties. Douglas County, which includes Omaha, voted Democratic by 10.17 points and sits inside Nebraska's second congressional district, one of the most competitive House districts in the country. In Nebraska, one of the nation's most reliably Republican states, GOP Senator Pete Ricketts is seeking a full term against independent challenger Dan Osborn, a mechanic and labor leader who mounted a surprisingly strong Senate bid in 2024. The race effectively became a two-way contest after the Democratic nominee withdrew. Meanwhile, Cumberland County in Maine backed Harris by 35.30 points and remains a major vote-producing county in a state expected to host another closely watched Senate contest. Republican Senator Susan Collins is seeking another term against former Maine Senate president Troy Jackson, who has emerged as Democrats' leading candidate after Graham Platner suspended his campaign. Where Trump's Coalition Faces Its Biggest Tests One recurring theme in the research was the importance of counties where Trump prevailed, but only narrowly. Those communities may offer some of the clearest clues about whether Democrats are making gains or Republicans are consolidating their 2024 coalition. Examples include: A Republican campaign strategist told Newsweek that many of the counties identified in the analysis were carried by Trump in 2024, arguing that the president's continued popularity among Republican voters remains a significant factor in the political landscape heading into the midterms. What the Special-Election Map Suggests Another layer in the project came from special-election performance. According to Ballotpedia, party-control changes in state legislative special elections since 2025 have occurred in states including Florida, Arkansas, Georgia, Iowa, Pennsylvania, Texas, New Hampshire and Mississippi. The analysis does not assume those outcomes will automatically translate into congressional or Senate races, but they provide clues about where political energy and voter engagement may be shifting. Because special elections often occur in lower-turnout environments, they should be treated as signals rather than forecasts. Even so, they offer one of the few real-world tests of political momentum between national election cycles. Democratic groups argue that the battleground is broader than many voters realize. Heather Williams, president of the Democratic Legislative Campaign Committee (DLCC), told Newsweek that "2026 is a once-in-a-generation opportunity to fundamentally shift the balance of power in state legislatures nationwide." Williams said Democrats had already "flipped 30 seats since Trump was elected" and were now building on that momentum ahead of November. She added that the DLCC is supporting "hundreds of must-win races around the country this November." The organization told Newsweek it is currently tracking more than 500 districts nationally and has identified more than 160 target races, arguing that the most competitive contests are spread across a much wider map than traditional swing-state narratives suggest. That assessment reflects part of the logic behind Newsweek's county-level approach. A separate Democratic strategist pointed to recent special elections as evidence that areas previously considered safe for Republicans could become more competitive when voters were focused on affordability and economic issues. What Happens Next No county decides a national election on its own. But modern campaigns increasingly revolve around identifying communities where a few thousand votes can change the balance of power. A Democratic campaign source argued that concerns about household finances and the cost of living were likely to be the dominant issue influencing voters in many of the counties identified by the analysis. Meanwhile, a Republican campaign strategist told Newsweek that while the party was confident in its position, it recognized the historic challenges facing the party in power. "Historically, whoever the party in power is underperforms in the midterms," the RNC campaign source said, adding that Republicans hope strong turnout among Trump supporters can help offset those headwinds. As spending accelerates and candidates begin focusing their resources on the most competitive terrain, many of the counties Newsweek has highlighted are likely to become familiar names long before voters head to the polls in November 2026. Full List of 100 Counties Likely to Decide the 2026 Midterms Some counties were included because they sit at the center of competitive races, while others were included because recent special elections or local political shifts may offer early clues about broader electoral trends. Tier 1 – Core Battleground Counties Counties that appeared across multiple indicators (competitive House districts, Senate battlegrounds, close 2024 results and sometimes special-election relevance). Tier 2 – Major House and Senate Battleground Geography Important counties inside competitive House districts or major Senate battleground states. Tier 3 – Statewide Bellwethers and Major Vote Centers Large vote-producing counties that may say more about statewide movement than a specific House race. Tier 4 – Emerging Trend / Special-Election Signal Counties Counties that made the list because of special-election trends, unusual political movement, or broader electoral signals rather than because they're individually among the most important counties in America.
news.summary: Elections fought across America may be decided in far fewer places than the national map suggests, a Newsweek analysis has found.
news.author: Sam Stevenson

news.title: Filings admit US grant cuts
news.text:
WASHINGTON -- The Trump administration has acknowledged in court documents that it canceled $7.6 billion in grants for hundreds of clean energy projects "based solely on the political identity of the grant recipient's state" -- in this case, 16 states that voted for Democrat Kamala Harris in the 2024 presidential election.

The statement contradicts repeated assertions by Energy Secretary Chris Wright and other officials that the projects were canceled because they did not adequately advance the nation's energy needs or had other problems that made them a poor investment of taxpayer dollars.

Democrats and environmental groups seized on the court filing Friday, saying the administration had "weaponized" the federal government to kill good jobs and punish working families because of their political views.

"This administration has now admitted in court what has long been obvious: it terminated nearly 300 cost-cutting energy projects for no reason other than the fact that the states they were in did not vote for the president in the 2024 election," said Rep. Marcy Kaptur of Ohio and Sen. Patty Murray of Washington. Both are high-ranking Democrats on the House and Senate Appropriations committees, respectively.

"Weaponizing the federal government like this is outright un-American, and it's hardworking families already struggling with sky-high costs who are suffering the consequences of this corrupt abuse of power," Kaptur and Murray said.

They called on congressional Republicans to join them in holding the Trump administration "accountable for the President's failure to look out for all Americans."

The Department of Energy announced last October that 321 funding awards across 223 projects were terminated, saying that after review, they "did not adequately advance the nation's energy needs or were not economically viable."

The cuts, part of broader attacks from President Donald Trump on climate programs and clean energy funding, slashed federal support for projects to build battery plants, develop hydrogen technology, upgrade the electric grid and capture carbon dioxide emissions.

Russell Vought, the White House budget director, highlighted the cutbacks in a social media post, saying money "to fuel the Left's climate agenda is being cancelled."

The Energy Department did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Projects that were cut were located in California, Colorado, Connecticut, Delaware, Hawaii, Illinois, Maryland, Massachusetts, Minnesota, New Hampshire, New Jersey, New Mexico, New York, Oregon, Vermont and Washington. All 16 targeted states supported Harris, but Wright said the cuts were "business decisions" based on whether the projects were a good use of taxpayer money or not.

The cuts were immediately challenged in court, and more than two dozen Democratic members of Congress, led by Sens. Adam Schiff and Alex Padilla and Rep. Zoe Lofgren of California, wrote a letter to the Energy Department's acting inspector general requesting a formal investigation. The department's internal watchdog launched an investigation in December.

Government lawyers had previously confirmed in a court filing late last year that the selection of grants in fact "was influenced by whether a grantee's address was located in a State that tends to elect ... Democratic candidates in state and national elections (so-called "Blue States")."

That filing came in a separate suit filed by clean energy groups and the city of St. Paul, Minn., over the canceled funding. The most recent admission came in a case called Thakur v. Trump that's been ongoing since last spring. Federal lawyers acknowledged that they used keywords related to diversity, gender, vaccine hesitancy and COVID-19 to screen for projects that ran afoul of the Trump administration's priorities.

Holly Bender, chief program officer for the Sierra Club, said the latest court filing shows "the Trump administration is brazenly admitting to a vindictive approach to canceling much-needed energy infrastructure that ignores the job losses, air pollution and increasing bills that people are experiencing everywhere."

Instead of "building the energy projects we desperately need," billions of American taxpayer dollars are "going to line the pockets of a small handful of fossil fuel company CEOs," Bender said, citing nearly $3 billion pledged by the Trump administration to cancel offshore wind projects in favor of fossil fuel projects such as natural gas and coal.

news.title: Katy Perry condemns White House's use of Firework: 'A complete violation of everything my song stands for'
news.text: Dubai: The White House's official TikTok account posted a nine-second video on Thursday showing footage described as military strikes. The clip arrived as the latest in a string of official government social posts documenting the conflict, using black-and-white footage of explosions as its visual backdrop.What made the video stand out wasn't the footage itself, but the soundtrack. The clip was set to Katy Perry's 2010 hit "Firework," edited so that the song's signature "boom, boom, boom" lyric landed directly over the moment of impact in the footage, a pairing that read to many viewers as deliberate rather than coincidental.Perry's responsePerry addressed the White House directly on X two days later. "I am deeply appalled and angry to see 'Firework' used on the @WhiteHouse TikTok account as a backing track for video footage of military strikes," she wrote. "I did not approve this, I was not asked, and I absolutely do not condone it.".She followed that with an explanation of what the song had originally been written to represent. "I wrote this song to be an anthem of hope, healing, and inner strength for people going through their darkest personal moments," she said, describing its use in the video as "a complete violation of everything my song stands for." She closed her statement plainly: "My music is for bringing people together, not celebrating warfare."Why she doesn't actually control the song anymorePerry's objection comes with a complicating wrinkle that's drawn plenty of attention online. In 2023, she sold the master recordings and publishing rights to five of her albums, including Teenage Dream, home to "Firework," to Litmus Music, in a deal reported at $225 million.That sale means the legal right to license the song for use in videos like this one likely no longer sits with Perry directly. Her objection, then, isn't really a legal claim, it's a personal one, about how a song she wrote is being used, regardless of who currently owns the paperwork behind it.Part of a wider patternPerry isn't the first artist to publicly push back on how the Trump administration has used their music in official government content. Ariana Grande objected after her song "Bye" appeared in a White House video, writing that her music shouldn't be linked to what she called "this barbaric, inhumane, heinous nonsense." Sabrina Carpenter responded similarly after "Juno" was used to soundtrack footage of arrests, telling the administration directly not to involve her or her music in what she described as "your inhumane agenda." Olivia Rodrigo and the Rolling Stones have also objected to unauthorised use of their work in official content.That's a slightly different issue from a separate, longer-running dispute. Artists including Bruce Springsteen, Neil Young, Adele and Rihanna have objected in the past to Trump playing their music at campaign rallies, a pattern that predates this current wave of complaints about official government social media accounts specifically.Perry has a had long history of Democratic political involvement, having endorsed Hillary Clinton, Joe Biden and Kamala Harris across successive presidential elections, a history that's shaped how both sides have chosen to frame her statement..Katy Perry sparkles at FIFA World Cup 2026 opener, shares emotional stage moment with young Norwegian singer.Katy Perry reacts to Justin Bieber's Coachella performance: 'Thank God he has Premium...
